title: MV2: Multi-View Multi-Vehicle Driving Dataset for Novel View Synthesis
summary: Differentiable rendering has advanced novel view synthesis (NVS), yet applying it to real-world driving remains difficult due to sparse capture viewpoints, dynamic objects, and limited multi-trajectory data. We introduce the Multi-View Multi-Vehicle (MV2) dataset and benchmark for evaluating NVS models under large viewpoint changes in dynamic urban scenes. MV2 features synchronized captures from a car, scooter, and drone, each following distinct yet synchronized trajectories. Training NVS methods on one vehicle's camera stream and testing on another enables evaluation under substantially larger viewpoint variations than existing single-trajectory datasets. All sequences are registered via Structure-from-Motion and camera poses verified using manual pixel-level correspondence annotations, yielding 50 high-quality scenes with 12000 images. Benchmarking recent NVS and camera pose estimation methods shows that NVS performance degrades with increasing viewpoint disparity, and that feed-forward pose estimators notably lag behind optimization-based approaches, highlighting MV2 as a rigorous testbed for NVS in driving. The dataset, benchmark protocol, and project resources are available at https://mv2-dataset.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Introduces MV2, a multi-view multi-vehicle dataset and benchmark for evaluating novel view synthesis under large viewpoint changes in dynamic urban driving scenes, featuring synchronized captures from car, scooter, and drone trajectories.
AI.motivation: Applying differentiable rendering-based NVS to real-world driving is challenging due to sparse capture viewpoints, dynamic objects, and limited multi-trajectory data, and existing single-trajectory datasets cannot evaluate performance under large viewpoint variations.
AI.method: Constructs the MV2 dataset with synchronized captures from three vehicles (car, scooter, drone) on distinct trajectories, registers sequences via Structure-from-Motion with manual pixel-level verification, and benchmarks NVS methods by training on one vehicle's camera stream and testing on another.
AI.result: Benchmarking shows NVS performance degrades with increasing viewpoint disparity, and feed-forward pose estimators lag significantly behind optimization-based approaches, validating MV2 as a rigorous testbed for NVS in driving.
AI.conclusion: MV2 provides a rigorous dataset and benchmark enabling evaluation of NVS models under substantially larger viewpoint changes than existing datasets, with resources publicly available.

title: HIMEC: Directional Change Representation and Fixed-Interface Decoding for Remote Sensing Image Change Captioning
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing (TGRS) for review
summary: Remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) converts bitemporal imagery into a sentence describing semantic changes. Most RSICC methods condition caption decoders directly on fused visual features, leaving intermediate change structure and decoder-interface consistency less studied. We present HIMEC, combining Directional Change Representation (DCR) with fixed-interface decoding. DCR separates signed differences into appearance-oriented, disappearance-oriented, and shared-context streams before fusion. A learned-query encoder converts the fused representation into visually conditioned change-query tokens that form the scene decoder's only sample-dependent memory. A training-only auxiliary phrase decoder supplies caption-derived supervision. With a fixed zero input, the scene decoder maintains the same interface during training and inference. Separately, we evaluate a local-to-scene cascade conditioned on teacher-forced local states during training and autoregressive states at inference. On changed LEVIR-CC validation pairs, these states have a mean cosine distance of 0.69. Regime-matched conditioning recovers most of the associated deficit, whereas permuting state correspondence causes no detectable penalty. These findings are limited to the evaluated cascade. In a matched three-seed comparison, HIMEC reaches a Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation (CIDEr) score of $142.81\pm0.60$ on LEVIR-CC, versus $139.51\pm3.40$ for direct fused-feature memory. On SECOND-CC, fixed-zero and regime-matched diagnostic conditioning reach 75.67 and 76.99 CIDEr, respectively, versus 60.77 for the mismatched cascade. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/ayshaashra/HIMEC upon publication.

AI.tldr: HIMEC is a remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) method that introduces Directional Change Representation (DCR), which separates signed differences into appearance-oriented, disappearance-oriented, and shared-context streams, paired with a fixed-interface decoding scheme using learned-query encoding. The scene decoder receives visually conditioned change-query tokens as its only sample-dependent memory, while a training-only auxiliary phrase decoder provides supervision. Evaluations show that regime-matched conditioning (fixed-zero) outperforms mismatched cascade conditioning, and HIMEC achieves CIDEr of 142.81 on LEVIR-CC and 75.67/76.99 on SECOND-CC.
AI.motivation: Most RSICC methods condition caption decoders directly on fused visual features, leaving intermediate change structure and decoder-interface consistency less studied. The paper aims to address both gaps by explicitly modeling directional change components and ensuring consistent decoder conditioning between training and inference.
AI.method: HIMEC combines Directional Change Representation (DCR) with fixed-interface decoding. DCR separates signed differences into appearance-oriented, disappearance-oriented, and shared-context streams before fusion. A learned-query encoder converts the fused representation into visually conditioned change-query tokens used as the scene decoder's only sample-dependent memory. A training-only auxiliary phrase decoder supplies caption-derived supervision. During training and inference, the scene decoder uses a fixed zero input maintaining the same interface. A separate local-to-scene cascade is evaluated where training uses teacher-forced local states and inference uses autoregressive states.
AI.result: On changed LEVIR-CC validation pairs, teacher-forced and autoregressive cascade states have a mean cosine distance of 0.69. Regime-matched conditioning recovers most of the associated deficit, while permuting state correspondence causes no detectable penalty. In a matched three-seed comparison, HIMEC achieves CIDEr 142.81±0.60 on LEVIR-CC versus 139.51±3.40 for direct fused-feature memory. On SECOND-CC, fixed-zero and regime-matched diagnostic conditioning reach 75.67 and 76.99 CIDEr, respectively, versus 60.77 for the mismatched cascade.
AI.conclusion: HIMEC demonstrates that explicitly modeling directional change structure combined with fixed-interface decoding improves RSICC performance. The findings on regime-mismatch highlight the importance of consistent decoder conditioning, though the authors note these findings are limited to the evaluated cascade. Source code will be made publicly available.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Assess Proxemic Risk from Egocentric Robot Images?
comment: Accepted at the EMR 2026 workshop at ECCV 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Assessing proxemic danger from a robot's egocentric perspective is critical for safe embodied navigation in human environments and requires both visual and contextual reasoning. We evaluate three opensource vision-language models (VLMs) (\textit{InternVL}, \textit{Qwen-VL}, and \textit{SmolVLM}) on the classification of egocentric robot images into four danger levels, comparing three prompting strategies and two rounds of QLoRA fine-tuning against a stratified random baseline. Without fine-tuning, all models perform near the baseline, while fine-tuning yields only modest overall improvements. However, \textit{Qwen-VL} with an advanced prompt achieves substantially higher recall for high-danger cases than the other models. An analysis of person localization further shows that correct danger classification does not correspond to better spatial grounding, indicating that a model may produce a useful safety label without attending to the relevant region of the scene. These results show that current VLMs remain limited in fine-grained proxemic reasoning and spatial grounding, although targeted prompting and fine-tuning can improve high-danger detection in selected models.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates three open-source vision-language models (InternVL, Qwen-VL, SmolVLM) on classifying egocentric robot images into four proxemic danger levels, testing three prompting strategies and two rounds of QLoRA fine-tuning. Results show minimal gains from fine-tuning overall, though Qwen-VL with advanced prompting achieves notably higher recall for high-danger cases. Critically, correct danger classification does not correlate with spatial grounding accuracy, revealing that VLMs can output useful safety labels without attending to relevant scene regions.
AI.motivation: Assessing proxemic danger from a robot's egocentric view is essential for safe embodied navigation in human environments, requiring both visual and contextual reasoning. The study aims to determine whether current open-source VLMs are capable of this fine-grained reasoning task.
AI.method: Three VLMs (InternVL, Qwen-VL, SmolVLM) were evaluated on four-level danger classification of egocentric robot images, comparing three prompting strategies and two rounds of QLoRA fine-tuning against a stratified random baseline. Person localization analysis was also conducted to examine spatial grounding.
AI.result: All models perform near baseline without fine-tuning. Fine-tuning yields only modest overall improvements, but Qwen-VL with an advanced prompt achieves substantially higher recall for high-danger cases. Correct danger classification does not correspond to better spatial grounding.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs remain limited in fine-grained proxemic reasoning and spatial grounding, though targeted prompting and fine-tuning can improve high-danger detection in selected models.

title: Surface-to-Skeleton 3D Cephalometry: Estimating Hidden Skeletal Landmarks from CT-Derived External Soft-Tissue Surfaces
comment: Accepted to AI4M3D Workshop at ECCV 2026
summary: Existing 3D facial-landmark methods localize points on visible skin, but whether CT-defined internal skeletal landmarks can be inferred from external soft-tissue geometry remains unclear. We formulate a coordinate-consistent surface-to-skeleton task using same-acquisition CT-derived surfaces, separating estimation from optical-to-CT registration, scanner-domain, and acquisition-state effects, with coverage analyzed separately. From 240 clinical CT scans from two hospitals, we construct a locked retrospective protocol pairing CT-derived external soft-tissue point clouds with 21 skeletal landmarks and three visible soft-tissue landmarks. An integrated hierarchical point-cloud model achieves 2.97 mm mean radial error on skeletal landmarks and 3.03 mm on deep or surface-invisible landmarks in 40 held-out patients. Patient-mismatch controls support patient-specific signal beyond a fixed population configuration or global similarity alone, while coverage ablations indicate dependence on non-anterior geometry. Optical-transfer diagnostics reveal substantial coverage-related and global-configuration components, although deployable optical inference remains unresolved. These results answer the controlled feasibility question affirmatively and provide a basis for hidden skeletal landmark inference.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether CT-defined internal skeletal facial landmarks can be inferred from external soft-tissue geometry using a coordinate-consistent surface-to-skeleton framework with hierarchical point-cloud models, achieving ~3 mm accuracy in held-out patients.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D facial-landmark methods only localize points on visible skin, and it remains unclear whether internal skeletal landmarks defined by CT can be inferred from external soft-tissue geometry alone.
AI.method: They formulate a coordinate-consistent surface-to-skeleton task using same-acquisition CT-derived surfaces, building a locked retrospective protocol from 240 clinical CT scans (two hospitals) pairing external soft-tissue point clouds with 21 skeletal and 3 soft-tissue landmarks. An integrated hierarchical point-cloud model is used, with patient-mismatch controls, coverage ablations, and optical-transfer diagnostics.
AI.result: The model achieves 2.97 mm mean radial error on skeletal landmarks and 3.03 mm on deep/invisible landmarks across 40 held-out patients. Controls support patient-specific signal beyond population configuration, and ablations show dependence on non-anterior geometry. Optical-transfer diagnostics reveal coverage and global-configuration components, though deployable optical inference remains unresolved.
AI.conclusion: The controlled feasibility question is answered affirmatively—hidden skeletal facial landmarks can be inferred from external soft-tissue geometry within same-acquisition CT settings—providing a basis for future work toward deployable optical inference.

title: StrAD: A Streaming Method and Benchmark for Audio Description Generation for Long-form Videos
summary: Visual content is the dominant medium of communication, yet without audio descriptions (ADs), it remains inaccessible to blind and low-vision people. ADs narrate context-relevant visual events during natural audio pauses. Manually creating ADs is expensive, limiting coverage to a small fraction of available content. Most existing automatic AD generation methods frame the task as video clip captioning, requiring ground-truth timestamps and additional context cues such as character databases. Current benchmarks reinforce this framing, consisting of short video segments paired with automatic or task-mismatched annotations. We introduce StrAD, a benchmark for long-form AD generation on full-length videos spanning diverse genres such as movies, documentaries, short films, performances, and video games. We reformulate AD generation as streaming dense video captioning. Our approach processes full-length videos with a sliding window, inserting ADs into existing transcripts without ground-truth timestamps, and supports both fine-tuned models and zero-shot prompting of vision-language models. On the segment-level task with given timestamps, our fine-tuned StrAD-FT sets the state of the art on CMD-AD with 36.3 CIDEr (+10.0 over Shot-by-shot), establishes a reference point on StrAD (51.0 CIDEr), and remains competitive on MAD-Eval at 24.9 CIDEr. On the full-video streaming task, StrAD-FT reaches a SODA score of 2.4 against 1.1 for our zero-shot baseline StrAD-Zero, though both exhibit limitations in temporal localization and narrative coherence. While prior work has tackled full-video AD generation in an offline, multi-stage fashion, ours is the first streaming approach, generating ADs on the fly without ground-truth timestamps. StrAD makes progress on full-video AD generation measurable, a prerequisite for scaling accessibility.

AI.tldr: StrAD is a benchmark for long-form audio description (AD) generation on full-length videos, reformulating the task as streaming dense video captioning. It introduces a sliding-window approach that inserts ADs into transcripts without ground-truth timestamps, supporting both fine-tuned and zero-shot vision-language models. The fine-tuned model (StrAD-FT) achieves state-of-the-art results on segment-level tasks and establishes a reference point on the new full-video streaming benchmark.
AI.motivation: Audio descriptions are essential for making visual content accessible to blind and low-vision people, but manual AD creation is expensive and limited in coverage. Existing automatic AD methods rely on ground-truth timestamps and additional context cues, while current benchmarks are limited to short video segments with mismatched annotations. This motivates the need for a long-form, realistic benchmark and approach for full-video AD generation.
AI.method: The approach reformulates AD generation as streaming dense video captioning. It processes full-length videos with a sliding window, inserting ADs into existing transcripts without requiring ground-truth timestamps. The method supports both fine-tuned models (StrAD-FT) and zero-shot prompting of vision-language models (StrAD-Zero). A new benchmark, StrAD, is introduced covering diverse genres including movies, documentaries, short films, performances, and video games.
AI.result: On segment-level tasks with given timestamps, StrAD-FT achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMD-AD with 36.3 CIDEr (+10.0 over Shot-by-shot), establishes a reference point on StrAD (51.0 CIDEr), and reaches 24.9 CIDEr on MAD-Eval. On the full-video streaming task, StrAD-FT achieves a SODA score of 2.4 versus 1.1 for the zero-shot baseline, though both show limitations in temporal localization and narrative coherence.
AI.conclusion: This work presents the first streaming approach to full-video AD generation that operates on the fly without ground-truth timestamps, in contrast to prior offline multi-stage methods. StrAD makes full-video AD generation progress measurable, which is a prerequisite for scaling accessibility to more visual content.

title: Attribute-Conditioned Multimodal Slot Factorization for Controllable Fashion Retrieval
summary:
Fashion retrieval often requires satisfying multiple attributes at once, such as category, color, pattern, and demographic. Monolithic embeddings mix these signals into a single vector, making attribute-specific control difficult at retrieval time. Many existing semantic-ID methods provide discrete item codes, but these codes are typically optimized as item-level or residual addresses and do not expose named, independently controllable attribute slots.
  We introduce MM-slotgate, a multimodal slot encoder that factorizes Fashion-CLIP text and image embeddings into four named attribute slots. Each slot learns its own text-image gate, so visually grounded attributes such as color and pattern can rely more on image evidence, while taxonomy-oriented attributes such as category and demographic can remain more text-driven.
  On H&M, using a combined slot-similarity and slot-logit retrieval score, MM-slotgate achieves 0.7566 macro ConstraintSatisfied@10, outperforming equal-weight multimodal fusion (0.7142) and fCLIP text-only retrieval (0.4755). The largest gain is on color, which improves from 0.321 to 0.889 (+0.568 absolute), as the learned color gate assigns 57.4% weight to image evidence. The learned gates are interpretable without modality supervision: color is image-leaning, category is text-leaning, and pattern and demographic lie near the middle.
  The resulting slots also remain controllable: linear probes show no measured excess leakage beyond the label-correlation baseline, and quantized slot codes support targeted intervention, including a 15.3x lift for color. These results suggest that controllable fashion retrieval benefits from typed, attribute-conditioned multimodal slots rather than either a single global embedding or opaque item-level semantic IDs.

AI.tldr: MM-slotgate is a multimodal slot encoder that factorizes Fashion-CLIP embeddings into four named attribute slots (category, color, pattern, demographic), each with its own learned text-image gate, enabling interpretable and controllable attribute-specific fashion retrieval. It achieves 0.7566 macro ConstraintSatisfied@10 on H&M, significantly outperforming baselines, with the largest gain on color (+0.568) and interpretable gate weights without modality supervision.
AI.motivation: Monolithic embeddings mix multiple fashion attributes into a single vector, making attribute-specific control difficult at retrieval time. Existing semantic-ID methods provide discrete item codes but fail to expose named, independently controllable attribute slots.
AI.method: MM-slotgate is a multimodal slot encoder that factorizes Fashion-CLIP text and image embeddings into four named attribute slots, each learning its own text-image gate so that visually grounded attributes (color, pattern) can rely more on image evidence while taxonomy-oriented attributes (category, demographic) remain more text-driven. Retrieval uses a combined slot-similarity and slot-logit score, and quantized slot codes support targeted intervention.
AI.result: On H&M, MM-slotgate achieves 0.7566 macro ConstraintSatisfied@10, outperforming equal-weight multimodal fusion (0.7142) and fCLIP text-only retrieval (0.4755). Color improves from 0.321 to 0.889 (+0.568). Gates are interpretable: color gets 57.4% image weight, category is text-leaning, pattern and demographic are near the middle. Linear probes show no excess leakage, and quantized slots enable a 15.3x lift for color.
AI.conclusion: Controllable fashion retrieval benefits from typed, attribute-conditioned multimodal slots rather than either a single global embedding or opaque item-level semantic IDs, as MM-slotgate demonstrates improved performance, interpretability, and controllability.

title: PseudoMapLabeler: Confidence-Aware Pseudo-Label Generation for Semi-Supervised Online Mapping
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, Accepted at ECCV 2026 DriveX Workshop on Foundation Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: A critical challenge in deploying online HD map construction systems to real-world scenarios is the scarcity of labeled training data, which limits model generalization in diverse environments. To address this limitation, we propose a teacher-student semi-supervised learning (SSL) framework that generates high-quality pseudo-labels from unlabeled data through confidence-aware map refinement. Our approach first trains a teacher model on limited labeled data, then leverages Beta-distribution-based confidence maps to assess the reliability of predicted map elements across temporal observations. Unlike conventional filtering methods that discard entire elements, we introduce a spatial clipping technique that selectively preserves high-confidence regions while removing unreliable segments. The refined map elements serve as map priors that improve the teacher model's prediction accuracy on unlabeled data in a second pass. These enhanced predictions become pseudo-labels for training a student model from scratch, followed by fine-tuning on the original labeled data. Experimental results on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that our teacher-student framework with refined pseudo-labels improves performance by +6.1 mAP under a low-label regime compared to training on labeled data alone, offering a practical solution to the labeled data scarcity problem in online HD map construction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a teacher-student semi-supervised learning framework for online HD map construction that generates high-quality pseudo-labels from unlabeled data using confidence-aware map refinement, achieving +6.1 mAP improvement on nuScenes under low-label regimes.
AI.motivation: Labeled training data is scarce in real-world HD map construction scenarios, limiting model generalization across diverse environments. Existing approaches lack effective ways to leverage abundant unlabeled data.
AI.method: The framework trains a teacher model on limited labeled data, uses Beta-distribution-based confidence maps to assess prediction reliability across temporal observations, applies spatial clipping to selectively preserve high-confidence regions instead of discarding entire elements, refines predictions on unlabeled data in a second pass, and uses these pseudo-labels to train a student model from scratch followed by fine-tuning on labeled data.
AI.result: On the nuScenes dataset, the teacher-student framework with refined pseudo-labels achieves +6.1 mAP improvement in a low-label regime compared to training on labeled data alone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed semi-supervised learning approach offers a practical solution to labeled data scarcity in online HD map construction, demonstrating that confidence-aware pseudo-label refinement can effectively leverage unlabeled data.

title: From Visual Widgets to UI Code: Efficient Tool-Grounded Generation
summary: Existing screenshot-to-code systems face a trade-off between flexibility and controllability. Direct multimodal generation can hallucinate visible details, whereas structured pipelines reduce such errors through component-wise decomposition, predefined templates, and customized intermediate representations. These structures, however, introduce additional generative orchestration and restrict outputs to designs covered by the representation. We investigate whether selective tool grounding can improve the fidelity--efficiency trade-off of direct widget-to-code generation. We introduce \textbf{WidgetGen}, a lightweight tool-grounded framework that extracts observable text and color evidence, performs high-level layout and optional chart reasoning, and directly generates executable JavaScript XML (\emph{JSX}). This design reduces reliance on component-wise generation while avoiding a fixed UI schema. Across six multimodal models and \(1{,}000\) held-out widgets, WidgetGen outperforms direct prompting and the structured Widget2Code pipeline on most visual reconstruction metrics, with consistent gains in area, legibility, and style. Finally, reconstruction-derived image-code pairs improve six Qwen-family open-weight models across every reported metric through supervised fine-tuning. These results establish WidgetGen as a strong lightweight baseline and show that selective evidence grounding offers an effective alternative to extensive representation constraints.

AI.tldr: WidgetGen is a lightweight tool-grounded framework for widget-to-code generation that extracts observable text and color evidence, performs high-level layout and optional chart reasoning, and directly generates JSX—improving fidelity and efficiency over both direct prompting and structured pipelines across six multimodal models and 1,000 held-out widgets, while also providing reconstruction-derived data that boosts Qwen-family models via SFT.
AI.motivation: Existing screenshot-to-code systems face a trade-off between flexibility (direct multimodal generation, which can hallucinate) and controllability (structured pipelines with templates/intermediate representations, which restrict output scope and add orchestration overhead). The authors aim to find a middle ground that improves fidelity-efficiency without heavy structural constraints.
AI.method: WidgetGen is a lightweight tool-grounded framework that (1) extracts observable text and color evidence from the screenshot, (2) performs high-level layout and optional chart reasoning, and (3) directly generates executable JSX—avoiding component-wise generation and fixed UI schemas while still grounding generation in selective evidence.
AI.result: Across six multimodal models and 1,000 held-out widgets, WidgetGen outperforms direct prompting and the structured Widget2Code pipeline on most visual reconstruction metrics, with consistent gains in area, legibility, and style. Reconstruction-derived image-code pairs also improve six Qwen-family open-weight models across every reported metric via supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Selective evidence grounding offers an effective alternative to extensive representation constraints. WidgetGen establishes a strong lightweight baseline for widget-to-code generation, balancing fidelity and efficiency without sacrificing flexibility or relying on rigid structured pipelines.

title: EgoCITE: Context-Augmented Indexing and Time-Aware Retrieval for Long-Horizon Egocentric Memory
summary: Long-horizon egocentric memory transforms continuous first-person video and audio into a searchable record of past experiences. We demonstrate two bottlenecks in existing systems: indices built from context-poor captions are unreliable for agentic search, while retrieval ignores a question's temporal intent. To address both bottlenecks, we introduce EgoCITE (Egocentric Context-augmented Indexing and Time-aware Evidence retrieval), a long-horizon agentic memory framework for egocentric QA. EgoCITE comprises three components. EgoScheme uses local multimodal context to turn fragmentary video captions and speech transcripts into self-contained atomic memory indices. EgoIndex organizes complementary action, activity, utterance, and conversation representations into searchable multi-view memory indices at multiple granularities. EgoRetrv combines semantic search with question-conditioned temporal relevance scoring and curation of retrieved evidence. We evaluate EgoCITE on EgoLifeQA, EgoMem, and EgoR1-Bench in terms of answer accuracy and target-event retrieval alignment. EgoCITE improves accuracy over agentic memory baselines by at least 4.4--14.2\% while achieving 36$\times$ lower cost than long-context LLM agents.

AI.tldr: EgoCITE is a long-horizon egocentric memory framework for QA that addresses two bottlenecks in existing systems: context-poor caption indices unreliable for agentic search, and retrieval that ignores temporal intent. It comprises EgoScheme (context-augmented indexing), EgoIndex (multi-view memory organization), and EgoRetrv (time-aware retrieval), improving accuracy by 4.4-14.2% over baselines with 36x lower cost than long-context LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Existing egocentric memory systems suffer from two key bottlenecks: (1) indices built from context-poor captions are unreliable for agentic search, and (2) retrieval mechanisms fail to account for a question's temporal intent, making long-horizon QA over continuous first-person video/audio ineffective.
AI.method: EgoCITE consists of three components: EgoScheme uses local multimodal context to convert fragmentary video captions and speech transcripts into self-contained atomic memory indices; EgoIndex organizes complementary action, activity, utterance, and conversation representations into searchable multi-view indices at multiple granularities; EgoRetrv combines semantic search with question-conditioned temporal relevance scoring and curation of retrieved evidence.
AI.result: On EgoLifeQA, EgoMem, and EgoR1-Bench benchmarks, EgoCITE improves answer accuracy over agentic memory baselines by at least 4.4-14.2% and achieves 36x lower cost than long-context LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: EgoCITE demonstrates that context-augmented indexing and time-aware retrieval are effective and cost-efficient for long-horizon egocentric memory QA, outperforming existing agentic memory baselines while being significantly cheaper than long-context approaches.

title: Inference-Time Orthogonal Seeding Enables Geometry-Aligned 3D Organ Segmentation for Slice-Propagation Methods
comment: 8 Pages Accepted at MLMI Workshop MICCAI 2026
summary: Dense voxel-level annotation remains a major bottleneck in 3D medical image segmentation. Single-slice propagation methods such as Sli2Vol reduce this burden by propagating one annotated seed slice through a volume using label-free registration. However, axial-only propagation accumulates errors with distance from the seed, especially in surface-distance metrics, because it ignores coronal and sagittal evidence and therefore underuses the 3D information available in CT/MRI volumes. To better leverage volumetric geometry, we study how key training and inference choices affect slice-propagation models, including single-axis versus multi-axis label-free registration, single-seed versus multi-seed propagation, and orthogonal seed configurations. Instead of propagating from a single axial seed, we use three orthogonal seeds---one axial, one coronal, and one sagittal---and fuse their propagated labels with a simple label-free rule. Our results show that the training paradigm has limited impact: an axially trained network applied to off-axis seeds captures nearly all the improvement, while explicit three-axis training adds little. Instead, performance is driven by inference-time seed geometry, especially orthogonality rather than the number of annotated slices, as a budget-matched three-axial control provides no benefit and can even degrade performance. On a multi-organ CT cohort, orthogonal seeding with the axial Sli2Vol backbone improves Dice by 21.9%, Normalized Surface Dice by 25.5%, and reduces Average Hausdorff Distance by 53.5% over the single-axis baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper improves single-slice propagation for 3D medical image segmentation by using three orthogonal seed slices (axial, coronal, sagittal) fused with a simple label-free rule, showing that inference-time seed geometry—especially orthogonality—matters more than training paradigm or number of slices, achieving large gains over axial-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Dense voxel-level annotation is a major bottleneck in 3D medical image segmentation. Single-slice propagation (e.g., Sli2Vol) reduces annotation burden but axial-only propagation ignores coronal and sagittal evidence, accumulating errors and underusing 3D information in CT/MRI volumes.
AI.method: The authors systematically study training and inference choices affecting slice-propagation models, including single-axis vs multi-axis label-free registration, single-seed vs multi-seed propagation, and orthogonal seed configurations. They propose using three orthogonal seeds (axial, coronal, sagittal) and fusing their propagated labels with a simple label-free rule.
AI.result: The training paradigm has limited impact: an axially trained network applied to off-axis seeds captures nearly all improvement, while explicit three-axis training adds little. Performance is driven by inference-time seed geometry, especially orthogonality rather than slice count. On a multi-organ CT cohort, orthogonal seeding improves Dice by 21.9%, Normalized Surface Dice by 25.5%, and reduces Average Hausdorff Distance by 53.5% over the single-axis baseline.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal seed configurations with a simple fusion rule substantially improve slice-propagation segmentation, and inference-time seed geometry—particularly orthogonality—is the key driver of performance rather than training paradigm or number of annotated slices.

title: Mr3D-VL: A generalist vision language foundation model for Multiparametric 3D Magnetic Resonance Imaging
summary: Multi-parametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) is a cornerstone for brain tumor diagnosis and treatment, yet current AI models face critical limitations: their lack of natural language interaction and interpretability impedes spatial information integration and cross-modal reasoning required clinically. Key challenges arise from significant physical meaning differences across modalities, spatial misalignment due to scan intervals, and the need for complex multi-feature interpretation in tasks like glioma grading. While visual-language models (VLMs) show promise in cross-modal understanding, existing methods focus mainly on 2D image modeling, neglecting direct perception of 3D volumetric space. Although 3D VLMs have been proposed for report generation and feature alignment in 3D CT imaging, mpMRI applications demand collaborative inference across multiple imaging modalities-a requirement unmet by current solutions. To address this, we introduce Mr3D-VL, a dedicated visual-language foundation model for multi-parametric 3D MRI. With 4 billion parameters, it employs an unsupervised pre-trained shared 3D encoder and 4D rotational positional embedding for dual modality-spatial integration. Its cross-modal projection layer uses a multi-resolution feature implantation strategy to enhance feature perception across resolutions. Experimental results show significant improvements over existing 4B/7B/30B domain-specific and general-purpose models in text generation tasks, achieving a BERTScore of 0.856 for report generation, with question-answering accuracy at 0.713 and multiple-choice accuracy at 0.912.

AI.tldr: Mr3D-VL is a 4B-parameter visual-language foundation model designed for multi-parametric 3D MRI, featuring an unsupervised pre-trained shared 3D encoder, 4D rotational positional embedding for modality-spatial integration, and a multi-resolution feature implantation strategy for cross-modal reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance in report generation (BERTScore 0.856), QA accuracy (0.713), and multiple-choice accuracy (0.912).
AI.motivation: Current AI models for brain tumor diagnosis using mpMRI lack natural language interaction and interpretability, struggle with cross-modal reasoning, and existing VLMs focus on 2D imaging or single-modality 3D CT, failing to address the collaborative multi-modality inference and spatial alignment challenges inherent in 3D mpMRI.
AI.method: Mr3D-VL employs a 4B-parameter architecture with an unsupervised pre-trained shared 3D encoder for volumetric representation, 4D rotational positional embedding to jointly encode modality and spatial information, and a cross-modal projection layer using multi-resolution feature implantation to enhance feature perception across different resolutions.
AI.result: Mr3D-VL outperforms existing 4B/7B/30B domain-specific and general-purpose models in text generation tasks, achieving a BERTScore of 0.856 for report generation, question-answering accuracy of 0.713, and multiple-choice accuracy of 0.912.
AI.conclusion: The Mr3D-VL foundation model effectively addresses the multi-modality and 3D spatial reasoning gaps in mpMRI by integrating volumetric perception with language modeling, setting a new benchmark for cross-modal understanding in brain tumor applications.

title: Class Geometry as Supervision for Sample-Efficient Open-World Detection
summary: Open-world object detection requires models to recognize known categories, reject unfamiliar objects, and incorporate new classes over time. This is especially challenging in scarce-data settings such as biomedical and scientific imaging, where rare categories may have only a few annotated examples and fine-grained classes differ by subtle morphology. Prototype-based detectors are natural for this regime, but they typically learn class prototypes as independent anchors, ignoring relational structure among classes. We propose class-geometry supervision (CGS), a general framework that constrains learned prototype or class-representation spaces to preserve visual or semantic class dissimilarities estimated from training data. CGS introduces a dissimilarity-preserving objective that aligns pairwise distances among learned class representations with a target class-geometry matrix while retaining the standard task loss. We instantiate the same objective across prototype recognition, few-shot biomedical object detection, open-set detection, novel-class insertion, and OWOD adaptation on COCO. Experiments show that CGS improves sample efficiency in recognition and ova detection, substantially strengthens novel-class insertion, and improves unknown recall on COCO while retaining much of the known-class detection performance. Ablations show that meaningful visual geometry provides the most reliable gains, while random geometry can help novel separation but is less consistent for few-shot detection. These results suggest that relational class geometry is an effective supervisory signal for building calibrated and extensible open-world detectors under limited supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes class-geometry supervision (CGS), a framework that constrains learned prototype/class-representation spaces to preserve visual or semantic class dissimilarities, improving open-world object detection under scarce-data regimes such as biomedical and scientific imaging.
AI.motivation: Prototype-based detectors for open-world object detection typically learn class prototypes as independent anchors, ignoring relational structure among classes. This is particularly limiting in scarce-data settings where rare categories have few annotated examples and classes differ by subtle morphology.
AI.method: CGS introduces a dissimilarity-preserving objective that aligns pairwise distances among learned class representations with a target class-geometry matrix, while retaining the standard task loss. It is applied across prototype recognition, few-shot biomedical object detection, open-set detection, novel-class insertion, and OWOD adaptation on COCO.
AI.result: CGS improves sample efficiency in recognition and OVA detection, substantially strengthens novel-class insertion, and improves unknown recall on COCO while retaining most known-class detection performance. Visual geometry provides the most reliable gains, while random geometry helps novel separation but is less consistent for few-shot detection.
AI.conclusion: Relational class geometry is an effective supervisory signal for building calibrated and extensible open-world detectors under limited supervision.

title: Towards Sparsely Annotated Open-World Object Detection
summary: Real-world object detection operates under ambiguous supervision, where unlabeled regions may correspond to missing annotations of known objects or genuinely unknown categories. These challenges have been addressed separately in Sparsely Annotated Object Detection (SAOD) and Open-World Object Detection (OWOD). In practice, their co-occurrence remains an open problem. To address this problem, we introduce Sparsely Annotated Open-World Object Detection (SA-OWOD), a new task that jointly considers sparse supervision and the presence of unseen categories. We propose Dual-Perspective Object Discovery (DPOD), a unified framework that jointly models unlabeled known and unknown instances via two complementary mechanisms. The Known Target Recovery Module (KTRM) recovers supervision for unlabeled known instances and explicitly regularizes the feature space to separate known and unknown representations. Complementarily, the Dual-Disagreement Target Generator (DDTG) identifies reliable unknown candidates through cross-view semantic inconsistency. By integrating these modules, DPOD resolves contradictory supervision signals caused by ambiguous unlabeled regions. As a result, it prevents misclassification between known and unknown objects and stabilizes the decision boundaries. Experimental results on sparsely annotated open-world benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing open-world detection methods, particularly in detecting unknown objects.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Sparsely Annotated Open-World Object Detection (SA-OWOD), a new task combining sparse supervision with open-world detection. The authors propose Dual-Perspective Object Discovery (DPOD), a unified framework with two complementary modules: Known Target Recovery Module (KTRM) for recovering labeled known instances and Dual-Disagreement Target Generator (DDTG) for identifying unknown candidates. DPOD effectively resolves contradictory supervision signals and outperforms existing methods, especially in unknown object detection.
AI.motivation: Real-world object detection faces two intertwined challenges that have been addressed separately: sparse annotation (some known objects are unlabeled) and open-world detection (unknown categories exist). Their co-occurrence has not been jointly studied, creating an open problem where ambiguous unlabeled regions could be either missing known annotations or genuinely unknown categories, leading to contradictory supervision signals.
AI.method: The proposed DPOD framework integrates two complementary modules: (1) KTRM (Known Target Recovery Module) recovers supervision for unlabeled known instances and regularizes the feature space to separate known/unknown representations; (2) DDTG (Dual-Disagreement Target Generator) identifies reliable unknown candidates via cross-view semantic inconsistency. These modules jointly model unlabeled known and unknown instances to resolve ambiguous supervision.
AI.result: Experimental results on sparsely annotated open-world benchmarks show DPOD outperforms existing open-world detection methods, with particularly strong performance in detecting unknown objects while preventing misclassification between known and unknown categories.
AI.conclusion: DPOD effectively addresses the newly introduced SA-OWOD task by jointly handling sparse supervision and unseen categories. The integration of KTRM and DDTG stabilizes decision boundaries and resolves the conflicting supervision signals inherent to ambiguous unlabeled regions.

title: VOS-Agent: The 1st Place Solution for the 8th LSVOS Challenge (MOSEv2 Track)
comment: 1st Place Solution for the 8th LSVOS MOSEv2 Challenge (ECCV 2026 Workshop)
summary: Complex video object segmentation requires robust target propagation under severe occlusion, disappearance and reappearance. Although SAM3 provides strong promptable mask propagation, a uniform inference path remains unreliable for tiny targets with insufficient visual evidence and semantic-dominated targets whose identities depend on explicit attributes. To this end, we present VOS-Agent, a collaborative framework that retains SAM3 as the shared dense segmentation module and conditionally activates specialized agents according to target characteristics. A Target Perception and Routing Agent assigns each sequence to a regular, tiny, or semantic-dominated route. Tiny targets are supported by a Visual Tracking Agent through confidence-aware box prompts, while semantic-dominated targets are handled by an MLLM-based Semantic Agent through description-guided localization and candidate verification. On the MOSEv2 test set, VOS-Agent achieves 69.82% on the official $\mathcal{J}\&\dot{\mathcal{F}}$ metric and ranks first in the MOSEv2 Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge at ECCV 2026.

AI.tldr: VOS-Agent is a collaborative video object segmentation framework built on SAM3 that conditionally activates specialized agents (Visual Tracking Agent for tiny targets and MLLM-based Semantic Agent for semantic-dominated targets) based on target characteristics routed by a Target Perception and Routing Agent, achieving state-of-the-art results (69.82% J&F) and ranking first in the MOSEv2 Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge at ECCV 2026.
AI.motivation: Complex video object segmentation faces unreliable results with a uniform inference path, especially for tiny targets lacking visual evidence and semantic-dominated targets whose identities depend on explicit attributes. Although SAM3 provides strong promptable mask propagation, it cannot handle these diverse target characteristics robustly under severe occlusion, disappearance, and reappearance.
AI.method: VOS-Agent is a collaborative framework with three components: (1) SAM3 serves as the shared dense segmentation module; (2) a Target Perception and Routing Agent classifies each sequence into regular, tiny, or semantic-dominated routes; (3) tiny targets are handled by a Visual Tracking Agent via confidence-aware box prompts, while semantic-dominated targets are handled by an MLLM-based Semantic Agent using description-guided localization and candidate verification.
AI.result: On the MOSEv2 test set, VOS-Agent achieves 69.82% on the official J&F metric and ranks first in the MOSEv2 Track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge at ECCV 2026.
AI.conclusion: Conditionally activating specialized agents according to target characteristics improves robustness over a uniform SAM3-based inference path, effectively addressing tiny and semantic-dominated target challenges in complex video object segmentation.

title: A Generative Approach for Improving Multi-Label Defect Classification in Photovoltaic Modules
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of multi-label defect classification in electroluminescence (EL) images of photovoltaic (PV) cells. Training models on images where multiple defects co-occur creates learning ambiguity, making it difficult to disentangle visual features for specific defect types, a problem compounded by the scarcity of examples for individual classes. To tackle this, we introduce Generative Defect Isolation (GDI), utilizing the LaMa inpainting model with Fast Fourier Convolutions to remove selected defects and generate realistic, single-defect training samples. Extensive experiments on Vision Transformer (ViT-S, ViT-L) and EfficientNetV2-L architectures demonstrate that GDI significantly outperforms baselines. The performance gains are most pronounced in low-data scenarios; class-wise analysis shows substantial improvements, boosting the F1-Score for rare defect classes by up to 63.6%. Furthermore, GDI effectively resolves learning ambiguity from co-occurring defects, yielding a 26% reduction in such co-occurring classification errors. Our work establishes GDI as an effective method for maximizing the value of existing segmentation datasets and sets a new performance benchmark for multi-label classification in this domain.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Generative Defect Isolation (GDI), a method that uses the LaMa inpainting model with Fast Fourier Convolutions to isolate defects in EL images of PV cells, generating realistic single-defect training samples to address learning ambiguity in multi-label defect classification. GDI significantly outperforms baselines on ViT and EfficientNetV2 architectures, particularly in low-data scenarios, boosting F1-Score for rare defect classes by up to 63.6% and reducing co-occurring classification errors by 26%.
AI.motivation: Multi-label defect classification in EL images of PV cells suffers from learning ambiguity when multiple defects co-occur, making it difficult to disentangle visual features for specific defect types. This problem is compounded by the scarcity of examples for individual defect classes.
AI.method: The proposed GDI method utilizes the LaMa inpainting model with Fast Fourier Convolutions to remove selected defects from images and generate realistic single-defect training samples, thereby eliminating co-occurrence ambiguity during training.
AI.result: GDI significantly outperforms baselines on Vision Transformer (ViT-S, ViT-L) and EfficientNetV2-L architectures. F1-Score for rare defect classes improves by up to 63.6%, and co-occurring classification errors are reduced by 26%. Performance gains are most pronounced in low-data scenarios.
AI.conclusion: GDI is established as an effective method for maximizing the value of existing segmentation datasets and sets a new performance benchmark for multi-label classification of PV cell defects in EL images.

title: Dual-Manifold Geometry Guided Representation Learning: Adaptive Coupling between Kernel and Data Spaces
summary: Deep representation learning has primarily focused on how features evolve across network layers, while largely overlooking the structured geometry embedded in network parameters. We introduce a dual-manifold perspective in which each convolutional layer contains two coupled geometric spaces: a Kernel Manifold induced by convolutional filters and a Data Manifold characterized by intermediate feature representations. Because these manifolds share the same channel space, parameter geometry can provide complementary structural information to guide feature evolution. Based on this insight, we propose Kernel-Guided Feature Transform (KGFT), a lightweight module that derives a geometric guidance matrix from the kernel Gram matrix and uses it to transform the covariance structure of feature representations. Unlike conventional attention mechanisms that reweight feature responses, KGFT explicitly reshapes feature relationships by transferring geometric information from the kernel manifold to the data manifold. To accommodate network hierarchy, we further introduce Exploit and Explore modes with a depth-aware scheduling strategy and a learnable guidance strength that adaptively controls the contribution of geometric transformation. This design promotes geometric alignment in shallow layers while encouraging feature diversity in deeper layers, without imposing excessive constraints on representation learning. Theoretical analysis establishes the validity of the proposed transformation and characterizes its effect on feature covariance. Extensive experiments across CNN- and Transformer-based architectures, including ResNet, ViT, and LLaMA-7B, demonstrate consistent improvements on image classification and arithmetic reasoning tasks, validating the generality and effectiveness of kernel-guided dual-manifold representation learning. Code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: Introduces KGFT (Kernel-Guided Feature Transform), a lightweight module leveraging kernel manifold geometry from convolutional filters to reshape feature covariance on the data manifold, improving representation learning across CNN and Transformer architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing deep representation learning focuses on feature evolution across layers but overlooks the structured geometry embedded in network parameters. Since kernel and data manifolds share the same channel space, parameter geometry can provide complementary structural information to guide feature evolution.
AI.method: KGFT derives a geometric guidance matrix from the kernel Gram matrix and uses it to transform the covariance structure of feature representations. It introduces Exploit and Explore modes with depth-aware scheduling and learnable guidance strength, promoting geometric alignment in shallow layers and feature diversity in deeper layers.
AI.result: Consistent improvements on image classification and arithmetic reasoning tasks across ResNet, ViT, and LLaMA-7B architectures, with theoretical validation of the transformation's effect on feature covariance.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-guided dual-manifold representation learning is general and effective, transferring geometric information from kernel to data manifolds to enhance representation quality without imposing excessive constraints.

title: Dual-Stream Cross-Anchor Correction Grounding Long-Form Captions and the Domain Limits of Object-Level Anchors
summary: Object hallucination in multimodal large language models arises when language priors and corpus co-occurrence bias outweigh the visual evidence, with nothing tying an individual object mention to what the image shows. Most remedies intervene at decoding time without training, yet under a unified protocol their benefit is confined to short captions;supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a detail- rich corpus lengthens captions, but over forty percent still name absent objects. This paper proposes Dual-Stream Cross-Anchor Correction (DSCC). Unlike work that post-processes decoding, DSCC is the first to inject object-level visual anchors into the language model itself during fine- tuning: a perception stream aligns object-level hidden states at an intermediate layer to frozen text anchors by a bidirectional contrastive objective; a cognition stream lets deeper layers query those anchors by cross-attention at every generation step; and a two-stage curriculum gate couplesthem, making evidence retrieval a structural constraint at each autoregressive step. Under one backbone and one scoring protocol, experiments span long-caption hallucination, object-existence discrimination and cross-domain generalisation, with vanilla SFT on the same corpus and schedule as a length- and density-matched control, so gains are attributed layer by layer. DSCC is the only method reaching the long-caption, low-hallucination region: captions roughly 1.9 times the baseline length at 88.19% precision per object mention, the highest under a density-independent criterion. Ablations expose a synergy: the perception stream alone degrades precision yet reverses sign when stacked on the cognition stream. No universal superiority is claimed: three out-of- domain benchmarks yield a predictable, falsifiable domain-conditionality, the synergy being bound to the anchors' semantic domain and breaking on charts and optical illusions.

AI.tldr: DSCC is the first method to inject object-level visual anchors into an MLLM during fine-tuning via a dual-stream architecture (perception + cognition) with a curriculum gate, achieving long captions with low hallucination (88.19% precision per object mention, ~1.9x baseline length) while acknowledging domain-specific limitations.
AI.motivation: Object hallucination in MLLMs occurs because language priors and corpus co-occurrence bias dominate visual evidence, and existing decoding-time interventions only help short captions. Even supervised fine-tuning on detail-rich data leaves >40% of captions naming absent objects.
AI.method: Dual-Stream Cross-Anchor Correction (DSCC): (1) a perception stream aligns object-level hidden states at an intermediate layer to frozen text anchors via bidirectional contrastive learning; (2) a cognition stream lets deeper layers query those anchors via cross-attention at every generation step; (3) a two-stage curriculum gate couples the streams, making evidence retrieval a structural constraint at each autoregressive step.
AI.result: Under one backbone/protocol, DSCC reaches the long-caption, low-hallucination region: captions ~1.9x baseline length at 88.19% precision per object mention (highest under a density-independent criterion). Ablations show perception alone degrades precision but reverses sign when combined with cognition. On 3 out-of-domain benchmarks, performance is domain-conditional: synergy breaks on charts and optical illusions.
AI.conclusion: DSCC demonstrates that structural object-level evidence constraints during fine-tuning can effectively reduce hallucination in long captions, with the perception/cognition synergy being key. However, no universal superiority is claimed—the approach is domain-dependent, bound to the anchors' semantic domain.

title: Scaling Representation Diversity: Modulated Attention and Reconstructive Regularization for Visual Grounding
summary: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) is commonly studied under dataset-specific fine-tuning, resulting in specialist models with limited cross-dataset generalization. In this work, we revisit REC from the perspective of unified open-vocabulary grounding and identify representation degeneration as a key obstacle to scaling a single generalist model. To preserve representation diversity, we propose a holistic data-model co-design framework. Architecturally, we introduce the Modulated Attention-Contrastive Head (mACH) for efficient token-level vision-language alignment and a text-conditioned JEPA auxiliary stream that provides complementary gradient support to preserve alignment-active representations without inference overhead. On the data side, we introduce Objects365-Caption, enriching Objects365 with context-aware referring expressions for large-scale language supervision. We further provide a theoretical analysis showing that complementary gradient subspaces preserve alignment capacity and thereby scale representation diversity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our single-checkpoint framework achieves highly competitive performance on standard REC benchmarks while exhibiting strong generalization across heterogeneous grounding datasets without benchmark-specific adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) by framing it as a unified open-vocabulary grounding problem rather than dataset-specific fine-tuning. The authors identify representation degeneration as a key obstacle and propose a data-model co-design framework (mACH head + text-conditioned JEPA auxiliary stream + Objects365-Caption dataset) that achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks while generalizing across heterogeneous datasets without adaptation.
AI.motivation: REC is typically studied under dataset-specific fine-tuning, producing specialist models that fail to generalize across datasets. The authors seek to build a single generalist model and identify representation degeneration as the key obstacle to scaling, motivating a holistic approach to preserve representation diversity.
AI.method: The framework includes two architectural contributions: (1) a Modulated Attention-Contrastive Head (mACH) for efficient token-level vision-language alignment, and (2) a text-conditioned JEPA auxiliary stream providing complementary gradient support to preserve alignment-active representations without inference overhead. On the data side, they introduce Objects365-Caption, which enriches Objects365 with context-aware referring expressions. They also provide theoretical analysis showing complementary gradient subspaces preserve alignment capacity.
AI.result: The single-checkpoint framework achieves highly competitive performance on standard REC benchmarks while demonstrating strong generalization across heterogeneous grounding datasets without benchmark-specific adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-model co-design framework successfully scales a generalist REC model by preserving representation diversity through complementary gradient support and large-scale language supervision, enabling strong cross-dataset generalization from a single checkpoint.

title: PatchGen: Learning Soft Intra-Image Predictive Subsets for Visual Generalization
summary: Visual classifiers are expected to generalize under data shifts, target shifts, and their combinations, yet most existing methods focus on domain invariance while failing to address intra-image predictive sufficiency. We investigate the structural hypothesis that each image contains a sample-adaptive oracle intra-image predictive subset sufficient for label prediction, while the remaining patches form non-essential complementary context that may correlate with the label. The theoretical analysis shows that restricting prediction to this oracle subset preserves the Bayes risk achievable by the full-patch representation while admitting a complexity bound that tightens with the oracle-subset size. Based on this view, we propose PatchGen, a text-free module that learns a sample-dependent soft predictive-subset mask as a task-driven proxy for the unobserved oracle subset mask. Specifically, histopathology visualizations suggest that PatchGen assigns higher scores to tumor-consistent regions than to some frequently co-occurring inflammatory context. Extensive experiments on natural and histopathological image benchmarks spanning all three shift settings show that PatchGen improves average performance over matched-backbone baselines in most evaluated configurations, enhances generalization to unknown classes, and remains competitive with vision-language methods without text supervision.

AI.tldr: PatchGen learns a sample-adaptive soft mask to identify an oracle intra-image predictive subset of patches sufficient for label prediction, improving generalization under data shifts, target shifts, and their combinations without requiring text supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing generalization methods focus on domain invariance but fail to address intra-image predictive sufficiency, i.e., not all image patches are equally useful for prediction; some are complementary context that can hurt generalization.
AI.method: PatchGen is a text-free module that learns a sample-dependent soft predictive-subset mask as a task-driven proxy for the unobserved oracle subset mask, assigning higher scores to predictive regions (e.g., tumor-consistent areas) over correlated but non-essential context (e.g., inflammatory regions).
AI.result: Experiments on natural and histopathological benchmarks across data shift, target shift, and combined shifts show PatchGen improves average performance over matched-backbone baselines in most configurations, enhances generalization to unknown classes, and is competitive with vision-language methods without requiring text supervision.
AI.conclusion: Restricting prediction to the oracle intra-image predictive subset preserves Bayes risk while tightening complexity bounds, and PatchGen effectively approximates this via learned soft masks, offering a text-free alternative for robust visual classification.

title: CW-BASS v2: Saturation-Aware Pseudo-Label Selection for Semi-Supervised Segmentation under Foundation-Model Teachers
comment: Submitted to IEEE TPAMI. 22 pages, 11 figures, 17 tables
summary: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation has long turned on one question, which pseudo-labels to trust, and a generation of selection rules, dynamic thresholds, per-class curricula, soft confidence weights, answered it for the noisy, under-confident ResNet teachers of their day. Self-supervised foundation encoders change the regime: with a DINOv2 teacher, confidence saturates, so the filtering that helped a weak teacher can hurt a strong one. We propose CW-BASS v2, a saturation-aware pseudo-label selection method that reads the teacher's confidence regime rather than committing to one rule. It pairs held-out calibration, an unbiased per-class noise estimate, with a self-adaptive confidence floor that provably bounds retention away from 1, and combines them in a one-pass gate: measure the reliability of the teacher's confident set, pi_kept = Pr[correct | c >= tau], on a held-out slice, and filter strictly when it meets the confidence demanded (pi_kept >= tau), falling back to the adaptive floor otherwise. The boundary is the pre-existing operating threshold, not a value tuned to mIoU, and across six DINOv2 teachers it makes the correct strict-vs-floor call blind. CW-BASS v2 thus recovers the UniMatch V2 operating point on the saturated benchmarks by selecting strict (Pascal VOC 1/8 87.4 against its reported 87.9; Cityscapes within 0.5), and improves on it where the confident set is unreliable (pi_kept ~ 89%, ADE20K), where the floor edges ahead (+1.5 mIoU, single seed). The gate is principled because the failure it avoids is measured, not assumed: on a reliable, saturated teacher the confidence distribution's dynamic range collapses (98% of Pascal pixels >= 0.95), so an adaptive cutoff floods the retention mask and self-training decays into confirmation bias.

AI.tldr: CW-BASS v2 is a saturation-aware pseudo-label selection method for semi-supervised semantic segmentation that reads the teacher's confidence regime to decide between strict filtering and an adaptive confidence floor, rather than committing to a single rule. It uses held-out calibration to measure the reliability of the teacher's confident set (pi_kept = Pr[correct | c >= tau]) and filters strictly when reliability meets the demanded confidence, falling back to the adaptive floor otherwise.
AI.motivation: Traditional pseudo-label selection rules (dynamic thresholds, per-class curricula, soft confidence weights) were designed for noisy, under-confident ResNet teachers. With self-supervised foundation encoders like DINOv2, confidence saturates, making aggressive filtering that helped weak teachers potentially harmful for strong ones. The paper addresses the question of which pseudo-labels to trust in the new regime of saturated confidence.
AI.method: CW-BASS v2 pairs held-out calibration (an unbiased per-class noise estimate) with a self-adaptive confidence floor that provably bounds retention away from 1. These are combined in a one-pass gate: measure pi_kept = Pr[correct | c >= tau] on a held-out slice, and filter strictly when pi_kept >= tau, falling back to the adaptive floor otherwise. The boundary is the pre-existing operating threshold, not a value tuned to mIoU.
AI.result: Across six DINOv2 teachers it makes the correct strict-vs-floor call blind. It recovers the UniMatch V2 operating point on saturated benchmarks (Pascal VOC 1/8 87.4 vs reported 87.9; Cityscapes within 0.5) and improves on it where the confident set is unreliable (pi_kept ~ 89%), gaining +1.5 mIoU on ADE20K.
AI.conclusion: The gate is principled because the failure it avoids is measured rather than assumed: with a reliable, saturated teacher, the confidence distribution's dynamic range collapses (98% of Pascal pixels >= 0.95), so an adaptive cutoff floods the retention mask and self-training decays into confirmation bias.

title: SCOPE: Subspace Clustering with Online Per-Head Top-K Estimation for Sparse Video Attention
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) incur quadratic self-attention cost over spatiotemporal tokens. Existing training-free sparse attention methods often construct sparse masks from block-level or cluster-level proxy scores, which can obscure fine-grained differences among keys and miss high contribution keys under aggressive sparsity. Moreover, such proxy scores may yield overly concentrated softmax distributions, causing Top-$p$ to retain too few keys for some query clusters. Although a fixed Top-$k$ minimum alleviates this failure mode, a shared value cannot adapt to variations across heads and inputs. To address both limitations, we propose SCOPE, a training-free sparse attention framework that combines 3D-RoPE-aligned key subspace clustering with online per-head Top-$k$ estimation for efficient video-DiT inference. SCOPE partitions post-RoPE keys into temporal, height, and width subspaces, clusters them independently, and aggregates the corresponding centroid scores through lookup tables to obtain per key proxy scores for each query cluster. Building on existing hybrid Top-$p$/fixed Top-$k$ selection, SCOPE derives a head-specific Top-$k$ value online by averaging the initial retained key counts within each head, weighted by query cluster size, and selects additional keys only for query clusters whose initial retained key counts fall below this value. Sparse attention is then computed over the selected original keys and values. Across six model--task configurations, SCOPE consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines in both fidelity and latency, achieving up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end speedup on 720p HunyuanVideo with $28.46$ dB PSNR relative to dense attention.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a training-free sparse attention framework for video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) that combines 3D-RoPE-aligned key subspace clustering with online per-head Top-k estimation, achieving up to 1.99x end-to-end speedup on 720p HunyuanVideo with 28.46 dB PSNR relative to dense attention.
AI.motivation: Diffusion Transformers incur quadratic self-attention cost over spatiotemporal tokens. Existing training-free sparse attention methods use block-level or cluster-level proxy scores that obscure fine-grained key differences and miss high-contribution keys under aggressive sparsity. Additionally, proxy scores can produce overly concentrated softmax distributions, causing Top-p to retain too few keys, while a fixed Top-k minimum cannot adapt to variations across heads and inputs.
AI.method: SCOPE partitions post-RoPE keys into temporal, height, and width subspaces, clusters them independently, and aggregates centroid scores via lookup tables to obtain per-key proxy scores for each query cluster. Building on hybrid Top-p/fixed Top-k selection, it derives a head-specific Top-k value online by averaging initial retained key counts within each head (weighted by query cluster size), and selects additional keys for query clusters whose initial retained counts are below this value. Sparse attention is then computed over selected original keys and values.
AI.result: Across six model-task configurations, SCOPE consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines in both fidelity and latency, achieving up to 1.99x end-to-end speedup on 720p HunyuanVideo with 28.46 dB PSNR relative to dense attention.
AI.conclusion: SCOPE demonstrates that combining 3D-RoPE-aligned key subspace clustering with adaptive per-head Top-k estimation effectively addresses both the fine-grained key selection limitation and the Top-k adaptation problem, enabling efficient and high-fidelity video DiT inference without training.

title: Beyond Correctness: Benchmarking and Aligning Response Behaviors in Hybrid-Thinking MLLMs
summary: Hybrid-thinking multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow a single model to alternate between deliberative thinking and latency-efficient non-thinking inference. Although these modes differ in reasoning budget, their delivered responses should satisfy the same user-facing standard. Correctness alone may not characterize this response quality; we therefore evaluate task accuracy and response-pattern failures as complementary outcomes. We study this gap through \textbf{response-pattern alignment}: whether thinking and non-thinking interfaces preserve acceptable final-response behavior. We introduce \textbf{PatternEval}, a failure-enriched diagnostic benchmark comprising 2,415 multimodal prompts spanning visual perception and grounding, structured image understanding, and multimodal knowledge reasoning. PatternEval tests four recurrent failures: chain-of-thought leakage, response repetition, logical contradiction, and performative reasoning. Response-pattern failures are widespread across models from different providers, with non-thinking inference exhibiting substantially higher failure rates and thereby creating systematic misalignment between thinking and non-thinking interfaces. Motivated by this diagnosis, we develop \textbf{PatternRM}, a response-level reward model, and \textbf{PatternRL}, which introduces pattern-specific penalties during reinforcement learning. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B show that incorporating pattern-specific penalties into reinforcement learning can mitigate cross-mode misalignment while incurring a marginal task performance trade-off. Together, PatternEval and PatternRL provide an evaluation-and-training framework for aligning user-visible response patterns across hybrid-thinking interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses response-pattern misalignment in hybrid-thinking multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), where thinking and non-thinking modes produce outputs of differing user-visible quality despite similar task accuracy. The authors introduce PatternEval, a 2,415-prompt diagnostic benchmark for four recurrent response-pattern failures (chain-of-thought leakage, response repetition, logical contradiction, and performative reasoning), showing non-thinking inference has markedly higher failure rates. They then propose PatternRM (a response-level reward model) and PatternRL (pattern-specific penalties in reinforcement learning), demonstrating on Qwen3-VL-4B/8B that these methods mitigate cross-mode misalignment with only marginal accuracy trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Hybrid-thinking MLLMs switch between deliberative thinking and fast non-thinking inference, but these modes can produce responses that differ in user-visible quality beyond task accuracy. Correctness alone is insufficient to characterize response quality, so there is a need to diagnose and address response-pattern failures that create systematic misalignment between the two inference modes.
AI.method: The paper introduces PatternEval, a failure-enriched diagnostic benchmark of 2,415 multimodal prompts covering visual perception/grounding, structured image understanding, and multimodal knowledge reasoning, which tests four failure types: chain-of-thought leakage, response repetition, logical contradiction, and performative reasoning. It also develops PatternRM (a response-level reward model) and PatternRL (an RL training method that incorporates pattern-specific penalties) to mitigate cross-mode misalignment.
AI.result: Response-pattern failures are widespread across models from different providers, with non-thinking inference exhibiting substantially higher failure rates, creating systematic cross-mode misalignment. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B show that incorporating pattern-specific penalties via PatternRL reduces cross-mode misalignment with only a marginal trade-off in task performance.
AI.conclusion: PatternEval and PatternRL together provide an evaluation-and-training framework for aligning user-visible response patterns across hybrid-thinking interfaces, enabling more consistent response quality between thinking and non-thinking inference modes at minimal task-accuracy cost.

title: Erase but Preserve: Controllable Removal of Copyrighted Animation Characters via Optimized Semantic Anchors
summary: The exceptional generation capabilities of text-to-image diffusion models have raised copyright concerns, particularly the unauthorized reproduction of animation characters. Existing concept erasure methods fall short for animation character erasure: model modification methods struggle to identify suitable anchors for diverse, highly distinctive characters; prompt-based steering methods lack fine-grained control for precise intervention. These approaches often yield incomplete erasure and degraded image fidelity, hindering real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose a controllable method operating on the model's continuous textual representation to erase target characters during generation. We optimizes an anchor embedding via structural and detailed constraints to serve as a character surrogate, then replaces target-related embeddings with the anchor via a structure-aware adaptive strategy. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art erasure effectiveness and image fidelity preservation, while supporting controllable erasure degree, multi-target removal, and model transferability. Moreover, our optimized anchors are plug-and-play with current model modification baselines to improve their erasure performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a controllable method for erasing animation characters from text-to-image diffusion models by operating on the model's continuous textual representation, using an optimized anchor embedding and structure-aware adaptive replacement strategy to achieve state-of-the-art erasure effectiveness while preserving image fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing concept erasure methods fail for animation character erasure due to the diversity and distinctiveness of characters. Model modification methods struggle to find suitable anchors, while prompt-based steering methods lack fine-grained control, resulting in incomplete erasure and degraded image fidelity.
AI.method: The method operates on the model's continuous textual representation. It optimizes an anchor embedding via structural and detailed constraints to serve as a character surrogate, then replaces target-related embeddings with the anchor using a structure-aware adaptive strategy.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art erasure effectiveness and image fidelity preservation, supports controllable erasure degree, multi-target removal, and model transferability. The optimized anchors are also plug-and-play with existing model modification baselines to improve their erasure performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed embedding-space approach provides a more effective and flexible solution for animation character erasure in diffusion models, addressing the limitations of existing methods and offering practical deployment advantages.

title: Structured Local Differential Modeling for AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content has made the reliable detection of generated images an increasingly critical challenge. Existing detection methods are often dominated during training by semantically salient components with high signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), thereby suppressing subtler forensic cues associated with the underlying generation mechanisms and embedded in low-level statistical structures.
