summary: Implicit multimodal in-context learning compresses demonstrations into internal interventions, ranging from static task vectors to query-conditioned transformations and attention routing. Despite their common goal, these methods differ substantially in how the intervention depends on the query and where it modifies the model, leaving unclear which additional complexity is necessary for a given task. We propose the Selection--Realization Hypothesis. It views demonstrations as inducing a compact family of internal changes from which the query selects, while the model's computation constrains how the selected change can be implemented. We evaluate this account using controlled multimodal tasks in which query dependence varies without changing the underlying task primitives or prompt format. By contrasting correct demonstrations with matched counterfactuals, we measure the structure of explicit M-ICL and test whether it predicts intervention behavior. We find that the success of a static task vector is closely tied to how much of the demonstration-induced change is shared across queries. Additional intervention complexity becomes useful when explicit M-ICL contains query-specific or distributed structure that a local additive shift cannot recover. These relationships extend to natural VQA benchmarks and support cost-aware method selection without access to test performance. Our results provide a unified empirical theory of when demonstrations can be compressed into a task vector and when a more expressive intervention is warranted.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Selection–Realization Hypothesis to unify implicit multimodal in-context learning (M-ICL) methods, showing that static task vectors succeed when demonstration-induced changes are shared across queries, while more expressive interventions are needed when explicit M-ICL contains query-specific or distributed structure.
AI.motivation: Implicit multimodal in-context learning methods (static task vectors, query-conditioned transformations, attention routing) differ substantially in how interventions depend on the query and where they modify the model, but it remains unclear which additional complexity is necessary for a given task.
AI.method: The authors propose the Selection–Realization Hypothesis and evaluate it using controlled multimodal tasks where query dependence varies while task primitives and prompt format stay fixed. They contrast correct demonstrations with matched counterfactuals to measure the structure of explicit M-ICL and test whether it predicts intervention behavior.
AI.result: The success of a static task vector is closely tied to how much demonstration-induced change is shared across queries. Additional intervention complexity is useful when explicit M-ICL contains query-specific or distributed structure that a local additive shift cannot recover. These relationships extend to natural VQA benchmarks and support cost-aware method selection without test performance.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a unified empirical theory of when demonstrations can be compressed into a task vector and when a more expressive intervention is warranted, enabling cost-aware method selection.

title: Context-Matched Distillation: Teacher Causality for Autoregressive Video Distillation
summary: Interactive autoregressive video generation demands both low-latency rollouts and precise online control. Few-step distillation accelerates generation by reducing denoising steps, while online control imposes a causal constraint: frames and blocks should depend on history and controls available during generation. Existing video distribution matching distillation (DMD) pipelines, however, often supervise causal few-step students using bidirectional teachers that score complete clips. The score for a target can therefore depend on future frames and controls that were unavailable when the student generated it, misaligning teacher supervision with the student's causal information set. We introduce Context-Matched Distillation (CMD), a causal DMD framework that aligns teacher supervision with the information available when each target is generated. CMD replaces bidirectional full-clip scoring with a causal teacher that evaluates each target without access to future frames or controls. The same causal teacher initializes the few-step student, establishing a consistent causal formulation across teacher training, student distillation, and inference. Beyond aligning the temporal information boundary, Prefix Scoring matches supervision to the student's realized rollout context by evaluating each target under the cached student-generated prefix that produced it. Prefix Corruption further stabilizes training by perturbing unreliable prefixes produced early in training while preserving this target-context alignment. With a simple causal formulation, CMD naturally extends to frame-wise and chunk-wise generation, long video distillation, and camera-conditioned distillation. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art aggregate performance among autoregressive methods on both short- and long-video benchmarks, together with substantially improved adherence to time-varying camera controls.

AI.tldr: CMD is a causal distillation framework for interactive autoregressive video generation that aligns teacher supervision with the student's causal information set by using a causal teacher (evaluating targets without future frames/controls) instead of bidirectional full-clip scoring, extended with Prefix Scoring and Prefix Corruption for stable training and state-of-the-art results on short/long video benchmarks and camera control adherence.
AI.motivation: Existing video DMD pipelines supervise causal few-step students using bidirectional teachers that score complete clips, meaning the score for a target can depend on future frames and controls unavailable at generation time. This misalignment between teacher supervision and the student's causal information set is problematic for interactive autoregressive generation that requires low-latency rollouts and precise online control.
AI.method: CMD replaces bidirectional full-clip scoring with a causal teacher that evaluates each target without access to future frames or controls, and uses the same causal teacher to initialize the few-step student, ensuring consistent causal formulation across teacher training, student distillation, and inference. It adds Prefix Scoring (evaluating targets under the cached student-generated prefix that produced them) and Prefix Corruption (perturbing unreliable early-training prefixes for training stability). The framework naturally extends to frame-wise, chunk-wise, long-video, and camera-conditioned distillation.
AI.result: Experiments show state-of-the-art aggregate performance among autoregressive methods on both short- and long-video benchmarks, along with substantially improved adherence to time-varying camera controls.
AI.conclusion: Aligning teacher supervision with the student's causal information set via a causal teacher, Prefix Scoring, and Prefix Corruption yields superior performance for interactive autoregressive video generation and better online control adherence.

title: StreamTTT: Reconciling Real-Time Perception and Long-Term Memory in Streaming VLMs
summary: Humans effortlessly perceive the present while remembering the past, yet streaming VLMs often trade off real-time perception against long-term memory. Prior work shows that shortening the context can sharpen current-scene perception at the expense of long-range recall. To reconcile these abilities, we introduce StreamTTT, which writes long-range history into online-updated fast weights outside the attention context. This leaves a short sliding key-value cache dedicated to recent evidence, mitigating attention dilution. We train StreamTTT jointly on offline long-video QA and a newly constructed real-time QA corpus. On OVO-Bench, StreamTTT-4B outperforms SimpleStream-4B by 1.4 points in real-time perception and 3.7 points in backward tracing. It also remains competitive with the larger SimpleStream-8B on the Real-Time Visual Understanding (RTVU) subset of StreamingBench. Our code will be released.

AI.tldr: StreamTTT is a streaming VLM that writes long-range history into online-updated fast weights outside the attention context, leaving a short sliding KV cache for recent evidence to reconcile real-time perception and long-term memory. It outperforms SimpleStream-4B by 1.4 points in real-time perception and 3.7 points in backward tracing on OVO-Bench, and remains competitive with SimpleStream-8B on the RTVU subset of StreamingBench.
AI.motivation: Streaming VLMs face a fundamental trade-off between real-time perception (requires short context to mitigate attention dilution) and long-term memory (requires long context for recall). Prior work shows shortening context helps current-scene perception but hurts long-range recall, and no existing approach reconciles both effectively.
AI.method: StreamTTT writes long-range history into online-updated fast weights that exist outside the attention context, while maintaining a short sliding key-value cache dedicated to recent evidence. This design mitigates attention dilution. The model is trained jointly on offline long-video QA and a newly constructed real-time QA corpus.
AI.result: On OVO-Bench, StreamTTT-4B outperforms SimpleStream-4B by 1.4 points in real-time perception and 3.7 points in backward tracing. It also remains competitive with the larger SimpleStream-8B on the RTVU subset of StreamingBench.
AI.conclusion: Storing long-range history in online-updated fast weights outside the attention context effectively reconciles real-time perception with long-term memory in streaming VLMs, achieving superior performance over strong baselines without requiring a larger model.

title: Edit2TikZ: A Comprehensive and Challenging Benchmark for Scientific Figure Editing with TikZ
summary: Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown substantial potential in visual understanding and graphic code generation, editing scientific figures through code presents a greater challenge: a model must jointly recover visual structure, ground the requested change, generate compilable code, and preserve all unrelated content. While existing TikZ benchmarks mainly focus on figure reconstruction and generation, few systematically evaluate instruction-guided scientific figure editing with compilable code. We introduce Edit2TikZ, a comprehensive benchmark for scientific figure editing tasks, featuring 1,548 diverse and high-quality samples. Edit2TikZ combines real-world and controlled synthetic edit cases, supports both textual and visual localization request, and contains multi-step editing, each with step-level annotations. We further construct a human-aligned evaluation framework to measure whether a requested edit is completed while irrelevant content is preserved. Utilizing Edit2TikZ, we evaluate 14 mainstream MLLMs and find that current systems remain unreliable: on average, proprietary models achieve a compilation success rate of merely 75% and remain limited in both figure restoration and edit correctness, while compact models below 9B struggle further with instruction following and complete figure generation. Therefore, we build a mixed training set TikZEditMix and adopt reconstruction-then-editing curriculum learning for compact models. On Qwen3.5-4B, this training improves the compilation success rate from 45.35% to 83.40% and yields an average improvement of 18.7 points across our proposed evaluation metrics. The code and data will be released at https://github.com/Solunny/Edit2TikZ.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Edit2TikZ, a comprehensive benchmark for instruction-guided scientific figure editing via TikZ code generation, with 1,548 samples spanning real-world and synthetic cases. Evaluation of 14 MLLMs shows current systems remain unreliable, and the authors propose a mixed training set (TikZEditMix) with reconstruction-then-editing curriculum learning that significantly improves compact models' performance.
AI.motivation: Editing scientific figures through code is more challenging than generation because models must jointly recover visual structure, ground requested changes, generate compilable code, and preserve unrelated content. Existing TikZ benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction and generation, leaving instruction-guided figure editing systematically unevaluated.
AI.method: The authors construct Edit2TikZ with 1,548 samples combining real-world and controlled synthetic edit cases, supporting both textual and visual localization requests and multi-step editing with step-level annotations. They build a human-aligned evaluation framework measuring edit completion and content preservation. They also create TikZEditMix, a mixed training set, and employ reconstruction-then-editing curriculum learning for compact models.
AI.result: Evaluation of 14 MLLMs shows proprietary models achieve only 75% average compilation success and remain limited in figure restoration and edit correctness, while sub-9B models struggle further. Training Qwen3.5-4B on TikZEditMix with curriculum learning improves compilation success from 45.35% to 83.40% and yields an average improvement of 18.7 points across proposed evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs are unreliable for scientific figure editing via TikZ code, but the proposed Edit2TikZ benchmark, evaluation framework, and training strategy (TikZEditMix with curriculum learning) can substantially improve compact models' performance, making this a valuable contribution to the field.

title: UniTexture: Cross-Task Universal Adversarial Textures for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as generalist robotic policies capable of following diverse language instructions and performing a wide range of manipulation tasks. However, their direct control over embodied agents also exposes them to adversarial interference that may cause unsafe physical behaviors. Existing attacks on robotic policies are typically optimized for a single task or instruction, leaving the cross-task vulnerabilities of multitask VLAs largely unexplored. We introduce UniTexture, a cross-task universal adversarial texture attack that uses a single textured 3D object to induce targeted deviations in VLA action predictions across multiple tasks. UniTexture backpropagates gradients from the policy's action outputs to surface texture parameters through a differentiable renderer. It jointly optimizes the shared texture over a distribution of tasks, instructions, states, and viewpoints using a targeted action-space objective, steering predicted actions toward attacker-defined targets without optimizing a separate texture for each task. We evaluate UniTexture on OpenVLA and $π_{0.5}$ across diverse manipulation tasks and multiple evaluation settings. UniTexture reduces the mean task success rate from 90.0% under benign conditions to 48.4% under attack, induces target-aligned action shifts, and further exhibits cross-suite and cross-model transfer without re-optimization. Together, these findings reveal shared cross-task vulnerabilities in multitask VLAs that can be systematically exploited through a single adversarial surface texture.

AI.tldr: UniTexture is a cross-task universal adversarial texture attack that uses a single textured 3D object to induce targeted deviations in VLA action predictions across multiple tasks, reducing mean task success rate from 90.0% to 48.4% and showing cross-suite and cross-model transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial attacks on robotic policies are optimized for a single task or instruction, leaving the cross-task vulnerabilities of multitask VLA models largely unexplored. The authors aim to investigate whether a single adversarial surface texture can systematically exploit shared vulnerabilities across multiple tasks.
AI.method: UniTexture backpropagates gradients from the policy's action outputs to surface texture parameters through a differentiable renderer. It jointly optimizes a shared texture over a distribution of tasks, instructions, states, and viewpoints using a targeted action-space objective, steering predicted actions toward attacker-defined targets.
AI.result: UniTexture reduces mean task success rate from 90.0% under benign conditions to 48.4% under attack, induces target-aligned action shifts, and exhibits cross-suite and cross-model transfer without re-optimization on OpenVLA and π0.5.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal shared cross-task vulnerabilities in multitask VLAs that can be systematically exploited through a single adversarial surface texture, highlighting a new class of security risks for vision-language-action models.

title: Evaluation of Clinically Steerable Retinal Image Generation from Foundation Model Latent Spaces
summary: Medical foundation models learn latent representations of clinically meaningful phenotypes, yet their ability to support controllable image generation remains largely unexplored. We evaluate four retinal foundation models within the representation tokenizer framework and examine whether demographic and clinical information encoded in latent representations from foundation models is preserved during synthetic image generation. We show that generated representations and images faithfully inherit phenotype information when evaluated within their originating foundation models, consistently outperforming conventional latent diffusion on multiple downstream prediction tasks. However, these gains largely disappear when evaluated using classifiers trained on real images, revealing a previously uncharacterised synthetic-to-real representation gap. These findings demonstrate that foundation-model latent spaces provide a powerful substrate for controllable retinal synthesis while highlighting the need to better align synthetic representations with real-image distributions.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four retinal foundation models as representation tokenizers for controllable image generation, showing that generated representations/images faithfully inherit phenotype information within their originating models and outperform conventional latent diffusion on downstream prediction, but these gains largely vanish when evaluated with classifiers trained on real images, revealing a synthetic-to-real representation gap.
AI.motivation: Medical foundation models encode clinically meaningful phenotypes in latent representations, but whether these representations can support controllable image generation—and whether phenotype information is preserved during synthesis—has not been systematically explored.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four retinal foundation models within a representation tokenizer framework for synthetic image generation, and assess whether demographic and clinical information in latent representations is preserved during generation, comparing against conventional latent diffusion and evaluating with both originating foundation models and real-image-trained classifiers.
AI.result: Generated representations and images faithfully inherit phenotype information within their originating foundation models, consistently outperforming conventional latent diffusion on downstream prediction tasks. However, these advantages largely disappear when evaluated using classifiers trained on real images, revealing a synthetic-to-real representation gap.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model latent spaces serve as a powerful substrate for controllable retinal synthesis, but better alignment between synthetic representations and real-image distributions is needed to close the synthetic-to-real representation gap.

title: Fine-Grained Action Recognition with Cross-Attentive Latent Sparse Experts
summary: Fine-grained human action recognition (FHAR) must distinguish visually similar actions that differ mainly in body configuration, timing, or local appearance. RGB representations retain visual context but often suppress joint-level geometry, whereas skeleton representations encode kinematics but discard dense spatial detail. We introduce FineX, which factorizes fine-grained cues into RGB appearance, pose heatmap geometry, and skeletal-graph topology. Pairwise cross-attention enables symmetric, stream-preserving information exchange, followed by a streamwise latent sparse Mixture-of-Experts that routes each representation to a content-dependent subset of shared experts, regularized by a load-balancing objective. FineX achieves state-of-the-art results on Gym99, Gym288, and Diving48. On the long-tailed Gym288, it raises mean class accuracy from 68.6% to 76.2% (+7.6 points) without textual supervision or large-scale vision-language pre-training, demonstrating the benefit of structured visual-pose-graph fusion and conditional expert refinement for FHAR.

AI.tldr: FineX is a multi-modal framework for fine-grained human action recognition that factorizes cues into RGB appearance, pose heatmap geometry, and skeletal-graph topology, fusing them via pairwise cross-attention and a sparse Mixture-of-Experts module. It achieves SOTA results on Gym99, Gym288, and Diving48, improving mean class accuracy on long-tailed Gym288 from 68.6% to 76.2% (+7.6 points) without extra supervision.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained human action recognition requires distinguishing visually similar actions that differ in subtle body configuration, timing, or local appearance. Existing approaches are limited: RGB representations retain visual context but suppress joint-level geometry, while skeleton representations encode kinematics but discard dense spatial detail. Neither modality alone is sufficient for FHAR.
AI.method: FineX factorizes fine-grained cues into three complementary representations: RGB appearance, pose heatmap geometry, and skeletal-graph topology. It applies pairwise cross-attention for symmetric, stream-preserving information exchange between modalities, followed by a streamwise latent sparse Mixture-of-Experts that routes each representation to a content-dependent subset of shared experts, regularized by a load-balancing objective.
AI.result: FineX achieves state-of-the-art results on Gym99, Gym288, and Diving48. On the long-tailed Gym288, it improves mean class accuracy from 68.6% to 76.2% (+7.6 points) without textual supervision or large-scale vision-language pre-training.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the benefit of structured visual-pose-graph fusion and conditional expert refinement for fine-grained human action recognition, achieving strong performance without reliance on external supervision or large-scale pre-training.

title: SNM-VFI: Symmetric Nonlinear Motion-Guided Generative Video Frame Interpolation
summary: We propose Symmetric Nonlinear Motion-guided Generative Video Frame Interpolation (SNM-VFI), a training-free framework for motion-controllable generative video frame interpolation with pre-trained optical flow and video diffusion models. Unlike conventional diffusion-based VFI methods that synthesize intermediate frames from random noise, SNM-VFI guides the generative process with correspondence-aware frames produced by a symmetric nonlinear motion model. Specifically, we first utilize a pre-trained optical flow model to construct multi-frame nonlinear flow-based intermediate frames and confidence maps. These flow-guided frames are then encoded as latent priors to initialize and iteratively guide a pre-trained Video Diffusion model, enabling the diffusion model to preserve dense motion correspondence while improving perceptual realism. To further enhance output quality, we employ confidence maps to fuse structurally reliable flow-based predictions with diffusion-generated details in uncertain regions such as occlusions and object boundaries. Extensive evaluations on challenging benchmarks, including DAVIS, Sintel, and KITTI, demonstrate that SNM-VFI achieves strong perceptual quality, competitive reconstruction accuracy, and robust temporal coherence across diverse motion scenarios.

AI.tldr: SNM-VFI is a training-free framework for motion-controllable generative video frame interpolation that combines pre-trained optical flow and video diffusion models. It uses a symmetric nonlinear motion model to produce correspondence-aware flow-guided frames as latent priors, which initialize and iteratively guide the diffusion model, with confidence maps fusing structural and generative details in uncertain regions. The method achieves strong perceptual quality, competitive reconstruction accuracy, and robust temporal coherence on DAVIS, Sintel, and KITTI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional diffusion-based VFI methods synthesize intermediate frames from random noise, lacking motion correspondence control, which limits perceptual quality and temporal coherence.
AI.method: 1) Pre-trained optical flow model constructs multi-frame nonlinear flow-based intermediate frames and confidence maps. 2) Flow-guided frames are encoded as latent priors to initialize and iteratively guide a pre-trained Video Diffusion model. 3) Confidence maps fuse structurally reliable flow-based predictions with diffusion-generated details in uncertain regions like occlusions and object boundaries.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on DAVIS, Sintel, and KITTI benchmarks show strong perceptual quality, competitive reconstruction accuracy, and robust temporal coherence across diverse motion scenarios.
AI.conclusion: SNM-VFI effectively combines flow-based correspondence with generative diffusion, achieving high-quality video frame interpolation in a training-free manner without requiring task-specific training.

title: MLLM-Routed Heterogeneous Ensembles for Robust Cross-Dataset Image Classification
summary: Modern image classification models excel when trained on single task-specific datasets but often struggle to generalize across domains and difficulty levels. We propose ARMDIL, an Adaptive Router for Multi-Domain Image classification with LLMs. ARMDIL is an ensemble that uses a multimodal large language model (MLLM) agent to dynamically route each image to the most suitable vision backbone. Our diverse ensemble employs convolutional neural networks (ResNets), self-supervised representation learners (SSL), and vision-language models (VLMs), each trained on a unified label space constructed from multiple image datasets with differing distributions and characteristics. Empirical evaluations illuminate the distinct capabilities and vulnerabilities of each architecture across disparate visual domains. Crucially, we show that ARMDIL effectively navigates these trade-offs, performing competitively with specialized training-based routers. Furthermore, it drastically improves adaptability by allowing new information to be integrated via simple prompt modifications, while enhancing interpretability through natural language reasoning traces. These advances in cross-dataset image classification pave the way for more reliable general-purpose vision systems such as AI assistants and autonomous robots.

AI.tldr: ARMDIL is an ensemble framework that uses a multimodal large language model agent to dynamically route images to the most suitable vision backbone (CNNs, SSL, VLMs) for cross-domain image classification, achieving competitive performance with training-based routers while offering better adaptability via prompt modifications and interpretability through natural language reasoning.
AI.motivation: Modern image classification models perform well on single task-specific datasets but struggle to generalize across domains and difficulty levels, motivating the need for a more adaptable and reliable system that can handle diverse visual inputs.
AI.method: ARMDIL uses an ensemble of diverse vision backbones—ResNets (CNNs), self-supervised learners (SSL), and vision-language models (VLMs)—all trained on a unified label space across multiple datasets. A multimodal LLM agent serves as an adaptive router that dynamically selects the most suitable backbone for each input image.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations reveal distinct capabilities and vulnerabilities of each architecture across visual domains. ARMDIL effectively navigates these trade-offs and performs competitively with specialized training-based routers, while improving adaptability through simple prompt modifications and enhancing interpretability via natural language reasoning traces.
AI.conclusion: ARMDIL advances cross-dataset image classification by enabling more reliable general-purpose vision systems, paving the way for applications such as AI assistants and autonomous robots.

authors: L. D. M. S. Sai Teja
title: MapRoute++: Surrogate-Guided Semantic Routing for Visual Concept Unlearning
comment: Accepted at Unlearning and Model Editing Workshop, ECCV 2026
summary: We present our submission to Task 3 of the Gen$μ$ 2.0 Challenge on visual concept unlearning. Building on MapRoute, we introduce task-specific training objectives, richer concept representations, and semantic routing for concept-specific mapper selection. Our approach improves robust concept removal while preserving unrelated and semantically adjacent concepts. On the official benchmark, evaluated using the Erasing-Retention-Robustness (ERR) metric on Stable Diffusion v1.4, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline by 12.1\% on average across the five concept categories, achieving substantial gains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a submission to the Genμ 2.0 Challenge (Task 3) on visual concept unlearning, extending the MapRoute approach with task-specific training objectives, richer concept representations, and semantic routing for concept-specific mapper selection. The method improves robust concept removal while preserving unrelated and semantically adjacent concepts, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline by 12.1% on average across five concept categories using the Erasing-Retention-Robustness (ERR) metric on Stable Diffusion v1.4.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of visual concept unlearning in diffusion models, where the goal is to effectively remove target concepts while maintaining the model's ability to generate unrelated and semantically adjacent concepts without degradation.
AI.method: Building on the MapRoute framework, the approach introduces three key enhancements: (1) task-specific training objectives tailored for concept unlearning, (2) richer concept representations to better capture concept semantics, and (3) semantic routing that enables concept-specific mapper selection rather than using a single general mapper.
AI.result: On the official benchmark using the ERR metric on Stable Diffusion v1.4, the method outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline by 12.1% on average across five concept categories, achieving substantial gains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that combining task-specific training, richer concept representations, and semantic routing significantly improves robust concept removal while preserving unrelated and semantically adjacent concepts in diffusion models.

title: DreamX-Phi 1.0: Action-Conditioned Video World Model for Robotic Manipulation
summary: We present \textbf{DreamX-Phi 1.0}, an action-conditioned video world model for robotic manipulation that, given an observed frame, a language instruction, and a prescribed action sequence comprising end-effector poses and gripper states, predicts the resulting future observations. Yet realism alone does not guarantee faithfulness: a convincing rollout can still move the wrong arm or lose the manipulated object. To ensure the prediction respects each arm's commanded path, we inject per-arm $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ transformations into attention via \textbf{PRoPE-style geometric encoding}, preserving arm identity and rigid-motion structure. Action control alone does not fully constrain scene geometry or the evolution of small manipulated objects. We therefore add a lightweight \textbf{depth branch} for scene-level geometry and use \textbf{SAM3 masks} with a frozen \textbf{V-JEPA teacher} to maintain object consistency throughout grasping. We further distill the multi-step generator into a few-step student via distribution-matching distillation for efficient deployment. At the time of writing, \model{} achieves first place on Track~1 and second place on Track~2 of the WorldArena~2.0 Challenge. Our model and code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: DreamX-Phi 1.0 is an action-conditioned video world model for robotic manipulation that predicts future observations given an observed frame, language instruction, and action sequence. It uses per-arm SE(3) transformations with PRoPE-style geometric encoding for action faithfulness, a depth branch for scene geometry, SAM3 masks with a frozen V-JEPA teacher for object consistency, and distillation for efficient deployment. It achieved 1st place on Track 1 and 2nd on Track 2 of the WorldArena 2.0 Challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing video world models for robotic manipulation can generate realistic rollouts but lack faithfulness—they may move the wrong arm, lose manipulated objects, or fail to respect commanded trajectories. The authors aim to ensure predictions not only look real but also accurately follow the prescribed action sequence and maintain scene/object consistency.
AI.method: The model injects per-arm SE(3) transformations into attention using PRoPE-style geometric encoding to preserve arm identity and rigid-motion structure. It adds a lightweight depth branch for scene-level geometry, uses SAM3 masks with a frozen V-JEPA teacher to maintain object consistency during grasping, and distills the multi-step generator into a few-step student via distribution-matching distillation.
AI.result: DreamX-Phi 1.0 achieves first place on Track 1 and second place on Track 2 of the WorldArena 2.0 Challenge.
AI.conclusion: The combination of geometric action encoding, depth-aware scene modeling, object-consistency supervision, and distillation enables both realistic and physically faithful video prediction for robot manipulation, validated by competitive performance in a world model challenge.

title: TraVEL: Trajectory-Guided Video Embedding Learning for Driving-Video Retrieval
summary: Efficiently retrieving relevant clips from large-scale driving logs is essential for data curation, model development, and safety analysis. Structured and rule-based retrieval systems can explicitly target driving events, but typically require expert-defined rules, auxiliary data, and multi-stage perception pipelines. Multimodal embedding models offer a simpler and more efficient alternative by representing each video with a single searchable vector. However, general-purpose models often rely on shortcuts from static scene context and struggle to distinguish motion-centric events, such as turning left versus right or accelerating versus decelerating. In this work, we study how to adapt a general-purpose multimodal embedding model to driving-video retrieval. We first fine-tune Qwen3-VL-Embedding on paired clips and reasoning traces from nuReasoning using an InfoNCE objective. While this stage substantially improves overall retrieval, caption supervision alone remains insufficient for fine-grained motion understanding. We therefore introduce TraVEL (Trajectory-Guided Video Embedding Learning), a motion-aware fine-tuning framework that uses ego-trajectory similarity as a reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. Trajectories serve only as privileged training supervision; retrieval still operates on single-vector video embeddings without ego poses, expert rules, or auxiliary perception outputs. We further construct a driving-video retrieval benchmark from nuReasoning. Experiments show that TraVEL improves motion-centric retrieval across model scales: relative to SFT, it raises longitudinal and lateral mAP by 9.8 and 4.7 points at 2B, with corresponding gains of 7.2 and 1.5 points at 8B. TraVEL thus combines physically grounded supervision with efficient embedding-based search.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TraVEL, a trajectory-guided video embedding learning framework that adapts general-purpose multimodal embedding models (Qwen3-VL-Embedding) for driving-video retrieval. It uses ego-trajectory similarity as a reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve motion-centric retrieval, achieving significant gains over SFT in longitudinal and lateral mAP across model scales (2B and 8B).
AI.motivation: Efficient retrieval of relevant clips from large-scale driving logs is crucial for data curation, model development, and safety analysis. Existing structured rule-based systems require expert-defined rules and multi-stage pipelines, while general-purpose multimodal embedding models fail to distinguish motion-centric events (e.g., turning left vs. right, accelerating vs. decelerating) because they rely on static scene context shortcuts.
AI.method: The method has two stages: (1) fine-tune Qwen3-VL-Embedding on paired clips and reasoning traces from nuReasoning using an InfoNCE objective for overall retrieval improvement; (2) introduce TraVEL, a motion-aware fine-tuning framework that uses ego-trajectory similarity as a reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Trajectories serve only as privileged training supervision; retrieval operates on single-vector video embeddings without ego poses, expert rules, or auxiliary perception outputs.
AI.result: TraVEL improves motion-centric retrieval across model scales: relative to SFT, it raises longitudinal and lateral mAP by 9.8 and 4.7 points at 2B, with corresponding gains of 7.2 and 1.5 points at 8B. A driving-video retrieval benchmark was constructed from nuReasoning.
AI.conclusion: TraVEL combines physically grounded supervision with efficient embedding-based search, demonstrating that trajectory-guided reward learning can effectively enhance fine-grained motion understanding in driving-video retrieval without requiring ego poses or auxiliary perception at inference time.

title: GS$^{2}$CI: Robust Gaussian Splatting For Snapshot Compressive Imaging via Large Vision Model Priors
summary: Snapshot Compressive Imaging (SCI) offers an efficient solution for high-speed video acquisition and, under exposure-time camera--scene relative motion, multi-view scene capture by compressing temporal or spatial information into a single 2D measurement. While recent studies have explored SCI for 3D scene reconstruction, existing methods struggle with significant challenges due to information loss, limited viewpoint diversity, and the computational burden of jointly optimizing 3D representations and camera poses. In this work, we propose a novel framework that reconstructs high-quality 3D scenes from a single SCI measurement by leveraging 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the powerful priors of large-scale vision foundation models (VFMs). Our primary reconstruction combines measurement-derived 3D VFM initialization with SCI-aware Gaussian optimization. After coarse-stage convergence, an auxiliary 2D VFM provides pseudo-view supervision at synthesized viewpoints for local appearance refinement. To further address the instability caused by ambiguous SCI supervision during 3DGS optimization, we introduce Opacity-Guided Splitting and Growth Regulation (OSGR), an SCI-specific densification strategy that augments split candidates using local opacity statistics, discourages loss-compensating opacity inflation through mean-opacity regulation, and bounds representation growth with explicit candidate-ratio and Gaussian-count constraints. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves the strongest overall performance, combining leading reconstruction quality and robustness to viewpoint variation with competitive computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel framework for reconstructing high-quality 3D scenes from a single Snapshot Compressive Imaging (SCI) measurement by combining 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with large-scale vision foundation model priors, introducing an SCI-specific densification strategy (OSGR) to stabilize optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for 3D scene reconstruction from SCI measurements suffer from information loss, limited viewpoint diversity, and the computational burden of jointly optimizing 3D representations and camera poses. There is a need for a more robust and efficient approach.
AI.method: The framework uses two stages: (1) coarse reconstruction combining measurement-derived 3D VFM initialization with SCI-aware Gaussian optimization; (2) local appearance refinement using an auxiliary 2D VFM providing pseudo-view supervision at synthesized viewpoints. Additionally, Opacity-Guided Splitting and Growth Regulation (OSGR) is introduced—a densification strategy that augments split candidates via local opacity statistics, regulates mean opacity to prevent loss-compensating inflation, and bounds growth with candidate-ratio and Gaussian-count constraints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show the method achieves the strongest overall performance, with leading reconstruction quality and robustness to viewpoint variation while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the instability and quality challenges in single-measurement SCI-based 3D reconstruction by leveraging VFM priors and an SCI-aware Gaussian densification strategy.

title: TabSOM: A tabular-to-image encoding method based on self-organizing maps
summary: Tabular-to-image methods have emerged as novel approaches to leverage the high predictive performance of convolutional neural networks and vision transformers. They convert tabular data into image representations, mapping each feature at a fixed pixel location derived from a dimensionality-reduction method (e.g., t-SNE, UMAP, PCA). However, they encode only the marginal value of each feature and discard information about feature relationships. We propose TabSOM, a tabular-to-image encoding built on the Self-Organizing Map (SOM), which provides: (i) a spatial layout in which every input feature occupies a fixed canvas position derived from its component plane via collision-free Hungarian assignment; and (ii) a graph that captures pairwise feature relationships derived from the SOM component planes. The resulting image stacks two multi-scale node channels: one encodes feature values at fixed scales, while the other encodes pairwise feature interactions as spatial connections between related features. Two SOM-derived interpretability approaches are introduced: a prototype-inspired partial dependence plot and a class--separation importance score. Benchmarked against twelve existing tabular-to-image methods across public binary-classification datasets, TabSOM ranks first or second on every dataset and achieves the lowest variance of any method evaluated. Interpretability obtained with TabSOM was validated against Random Forest, XGBoost, and SHAP, the class-separation score shows reasonable agreement with established baselines on the top-ranked features while capturing complementary structural information from input data. These results demonstrate that TabSOM provides an effective and interpretable approach for applying deep learning architectures to tabular data, bridging the performance--interpretability gap in this domain.

AI.tldr: TabSOM is a novel tabular-to-image encoding method built on Self-Organizing Maps that converts tabular data into image representations preserving both individual feature values and pairwise feature relationships, achieving top-1 or top-2 accuracy on all benchmarked datasets while providing interpretability tools validated against established baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular-to-image methods (using t-SNE, UMAP, PCA) only encode marginal feature values at fixed pixel positions and discard information about feature relationships, limiting their predictive performance and interpretability when applying CNNs and vision transformers to tabular data.
AI.method: TabSOM uses Self-Organizing Maps to create a spatial layout where each feature occupies a fixed canvas position via collision-free Hungarian assignment from component planes, and constructs a graph capturing pairwise feature relationships. The resulting image stacks two multi-scale node channels: one encodes feature values at fixed scales, and the other encodes pairwise feature interactions as spatial connections between related features. Two interpretability approaches are introduced: a prototype-inspired partial dependence plot and a class-separation importance score.
AI.result: TabSOM ranks first or second on every benchmarked dataset against twelve existing tabular-to-image methods and achieves the lowest variance among all evaluated methods. Its interpretability results show reasonable agreement with Random Forest, XGBoost, and SHAP on top-ranked features while capturing complementary structural information from input data.
AI.conclusion: TabSOM provides an effective and interpretable approach for applying deep learning architectures to tabular data, bridging the performance-interpretability gap by encoding both feature values and their relationships while offering reliable interpretability tools.

title: SCULPT: Subtractive Composition for 3D Part Generation
summary: Part-aware 3D generation aims to create digital assets that are coherent as complete objects while exposing structural parts for editing, material assignment, animation, and reuse. Existing methods impose this structure outside the native generation loop: segmentation-based methods partition an already generated shape, while additive methods synthesize parts from predefined layouts, boxes, or tokens and then reconcile them into a whole. The former preserves the generated geometry but fixes the object before part boundaries are determined; the latter exposes part cardinality but often leaves shared boundaries vulnerable to gaps, interpenetrations, and material discontinuities. In this paper, we propose SCULPT, a framework that addresses these challenges through subtractive composition. Given a complete object represented in a structured 3D latent space, SCULPT iteratively applies a joint split predictor to generate one extracted part together with the remaining object. The predictor performs a coupled denoising process conditioned on both the image and the current 3D state, so the extracted part and updated remainder are generated together rather than reconciled after generation. The joint split predictor processes both outputs on the union of their native sparse 3D supports, allowing neighboring supports to overlap rather than imposing a disjoint voxel partition. The rollout ends when the remainder support becomes empty or reaches a fixed safety cap, allowing the number of generated parts to adapt to each object within that bound. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art geometry on PartObjaverse while preserving strong complete-object reconstruction after part assembly. Results on four dataset images, one text-to-image-generated input, and one real-world photograph further show fine-grained textured part decomposition beyond the benchmark.

AI.tldr: SCULPT is a framework for part-aware 3D generation that uses subtractive composition: given a complete object in a structured 3D latent space, it iteratively applies a joint split predictor to generate one extracted part together with the remaining object. The coupled denoising process generates parts and remainder jointly (not reconciled post-hoc), allows overlapping supports on the union of sparse 3D grids, and adaptively determines the number of parts per object within a safety cap. It achieves state-of-the-art geometry on PartObjaverse with strong complete-object reconstruction after reassembly.
AI.motivation: Existing part-aware 3D generation methods fall into two categories with complementary flaws: segmentation-based methods fix the object before parts are determined (preserving geometry but constraining structure), while additive methods expose part cardinality but suffer from gaps, interpenetrations, and material discontinuities at shared boundaries. The field needs a method that generates parts natively during the generation process while maintaining structural coherence.
AI.method: SCULPT performs subtractive composition in a structured 3D latent space. It iteratively applies a joint split predictor that performs coupled denoising conditioned on both the image and the current 3D state, generating one extracted part along with the remaining object simultaneously. The predictor operates on the union of native sparse 3D supports (allowing overlap rather than forcing disjoint voxel partitions). The rollout terminates when the remainder support becomes empty or a fixed safety cap is reached, making part count adaptive per object.
AI.result: SCULPT achieves state-of-the-art geometry on PartObjaverse while preserving strong complete-object reconstruction after part assembly. It also demonstrates fine-grained textured part decomposition on four dataset images, one text-to-image-generated input, and one real-world photograph, going beyond the benchmark scope.
AI.conclusion: By generating parts through subtractive decomposition within the native generation loop, SCULPT resolves the trade-off between geometric fidelity and structural part-awareness, producing coherent parts with robust shared boundaries and adaptive cardinality.

title: Alaya-EVOKE: From Linear-Scaling Supervision to Endless World
summary: Interactive world models must support persistent memory, responsive interaction, and long-horizon generation, yet these requirements place conflicting demands on the model. Maintaining history in the denoiser context or key-value cache incurs growing cost, forcing a trade-off between session length and retained memory, while low-latency interaction relies on few-step generation whose capabilities are bounded by its teacher. Evoke addresses both limitations by externalizing persistent world state and redesigning the teacher for long-horizon interactive generation. Scene geometry is maintained in an external, camera-indexed world state bank, from which only view-relevant information is retrieved, keeping the denoiser context bounded as the session grows. Rather than treating the teacher as a fixed generator, we design it for long-horizon supervision: its sparse attention combines chunk-wise grouping, retrieval of selected distant frames, and a linear-attention global state, yielding linear growth in memory and compute while enabling supervision over long horizons. Such supervision exposes content drift that stays locally plausible within short windows, while per-chunk conditioning enables prompt changes and event control throughout the sequence. A 30-second distribution-matching objective, applied under self-forced rollouts, transfers both capabilities to a three-step student that uses no classifier-free guidance, improving resistance to long-term drift while preserving responsive conditioning. With bounded context and recurrent external memory, Evoke supports open-ended, continuously evolving generation; on a single H200 at $384\times 640$, each $1.5\,\mathrm{s}$ chunk is generated in $2.11\,\mathrm{s}$. As a three-step world model, Evoke achieves state-of-the-art performance on WBench while remaining competitive on VBench-Long and VBench-2.0.

AI.tldr: Evoke is an interactive world model that externalizes persistent world state into a camera-indexed memory bank and redesigns the teacher with sparse attention (chunk-wise grouping, retrieved distant frames, and linear-attention global state) for long-horizon supervision. A 30-second distribution-matching objective transfers capabilities to a three-step student without classifier-free guidance, achieving state-of-the-art WBench performance with bounded context and linear memory growth.
AI.motivation: Interactive world models face conflicting demands: persistent memory requires growing context or KV cache (trading off session length vs. retained memory), while responsive interaction needs few-step generation whose quality is limited by the teacher. Existing approaches cannot simultaneously support long-horizon memory, low latency, and responsive control.
AI.method: Evoke externalizes world state into a camera-indexed scene geometry bank with view-relevant retrieval to keep denoiser context bounded. The teacher is redesigned for long-horizon supervision using sparse attention combining chunk-wise grouping, retrieval of selected distant frames, and a linear-attention global state (linear memory/compute growth). A 30-second distribution-matching objective under self-forced rollouts transfers capabilities to a three-step student with no classifier-free guidance. Per-chunk conditioning enables prompt changes and event control.
AI.result: With bounded context and recurrent external memory, Evoke supports open-ended generation. On a single H200 at 384x640, each 1.5s chunk is generated in 2.11s. As a three-step world model, Evoke achieves state-of-the-art performance on WBench and remains competitive on VBench-Long and VBench-2.0.
AI.conclusion: Evoke demonstrates that externalizing persistent state and redesigning teacher supervision for long horizons enables open-ended interactive generation with bounded context, linear scaling, low-latency few-step inference, and improved resistance to long-term drift, while maintaining state-of-the-art world model quality.

title: PlayWorld: Benchmarking World Models with Agent Players over Long-Horizon Objectives
summary: Video world models simulate future states conditioned on current observations and user actions. Recent systems have demonstrated impressive video consistency and action controllability over long sequences. However, fairly comparing these interactive models remains challenging. In practice, a human player typically evaluates a world model by pursuing long-horizon objectives through interaction. For example, a user may turn around 360 degrees to see whether the environment remains consistent, or walk into the water and inspect whether realistic water ripples are generated. The action sequence required to achieve the same objective may vary substantially between models, making fixed action-conditioned evaluation unsuitable for cross-model comparison. To address this, we employ multi-modal Agent Players to interact with world models toward specified long-horizon objectives. Building on this paradigm, we introduce PlayWorld, a benchmark providing 171 scenarios, each with a specified objective. To evaluate performance thoroughly, we assess models along four core dimensions: geometry consistency, interaction fidelity, out-of-sight evolution, and insight evolution. In addition, we incorporate basic ability metrics for video quality and controllability. Experiments across nine state-of-the-art world models reveal that current models remain unreliable on long-horizon interactive objectives, particularly in maintaining spatial consistency and persistent state evolution. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kxding/PlayWorld.

AI.tldr: Introduces PlayWorld, a benchmark using multi-modal Agent Players to evaluate video world models through long-horizon interactive objectives (171 scenarios across 4 core dimensions), revealing that current models remain unreliable in spatial consistency and persistent state evolution.
AI.motivation: Fixed action-conditioned evaluation is unsuitable for comparing interactive world models because the action sequences needed to achieve the same objective can vary substantially between models. A human-like agent pursuing long-horizon objectives through interaction is needed for fair cross-model comparison.
AI.method: Employs multi-modal Agent Players to interact with world models toward specified long-horizon objectives. Builds PlayWorld benchmark with 171 scenarios, evaluating along four core dimensions (geometry consistency, interaction fidelity, out-of-sight evolution, insight evolution) plus basic video quality and controllability metrics.
AI.result: Experiments across nine state-of-the-art world models show they remain unreliable on long-horizon interactive objectives, especially in maintaining spatial consistency and persistent state evolution.
AI.conclusion: Current video world models fall short of reliable long-horizon interaction, and PlayWorld provides a standardized evaluation framework to expose these limitations and guide future improvements.

title: V-RAE: Rethinking Video Latent Spaces for Generation
comment: 26 pages, 8 tables, 13 figures, project page: https://v-rae.github.io/
summary: Latent video generation relies on autoencoders to define a compact space in which generative models operate. Although video autoencoder architectures have evolved substantially, their latent spaces are still optimized primarily for pixel-level reconstruction and provide limited high-level semantic organization. A reconstruction-optimal latent space, however, need not be well suited to generative modeling. We propose V-RAE, a video representation autoencoder that builds compact generative latents on top of frozen vision foundation model representations. A lightweight temporal pooling module removes temporal redundancy while preserving semantic structure, and a video decoder reconstructs continuous motion from the compressed features. We evaluate V-RAE with four representative frozen encoders on video reconstruction, semantic probing, and class-conditional generation. V-RAE achieves 2.13 rFVD on K600, outperforming all evaluated large-scale pretrained video VAEs. Its latents retain substantially more semantic information than conventional video tokenizer latents. Under matched generation settings, our best variant achieves gFVD scores of 117.86 and 19.16 on UCF101 and K600, respectively, while converging up to 6x faster}. We further show that reconstruction quality alone is insufficient to characterize generative utility and introduce tFVD, a temporal-coherence diagnostic that correlates more reliably with downstream generation quality. Beyond video generation, V-RAE also improves future video prediction on Cityscapes over the Wan 2.2 VAE latent space under matched prediction settings. Taken together, the experiments show that frozen semantic representations can support video reconstruction, generation, and predictive modeling. The project page: https://v-rae.github.io/.

AI.tldr: V-RAE is a video representation autoencoder that builds compact generative latents on top of frozen vision foundation model representations, achieving superior video reconstruction, generation, and semantic retention compared to conventional video VAEs while converging up to 6x faster.
AI.motivation: Existing video autoencoders optimize latent spaces primarily for pixel-level reconstruction, but reconstruction-optimal latent spaces may not be well suited for generative modeling since they lack high-level semantic organization.
AI.method: V-RAE uses frozen vision foundation model encoders to extract semantic representations, a lightweight temporal pooling module to remove temporal redundancy while preserving semantic structure, and a video decoder to reconstruct continuous motion from the compressed features. It also introduces tFVD, a temporal-coherence diagnostic metric.
AI.result: V-RAE achieves 2.13 rFVD on K600, outperforming large-scale pretrained video VAEs, retains more semantic information than conventional tokenizers, achieves gFVD of 117.86 (UCF101) and 19.16 (K600) with up to 6x faster convergence, and improves future video prediction on Cityscapes over Wan 2.2 VAE latent space.
AI.conclusion: Frozen semantic representations can effectively support video reconstruction, generation, and predictive modeling, and reconstruction quality alone is insufficient to characterize generative utility—necessitating temporal-coherence diagnostics like tFVD.

title: AutoDesign: Meta-Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Design
summary: Transforming multimodal sources into condensed and structured media outputs can be fundamentally conceptualized as a long-horizon agentic process centered on a model-harness system. While an ideal harness system should align with human design priors and accumulate reusable experience through empirical exploration to drive recursive self-improvement, existing paradigms remain static and fall short of this capability. In this paper, we present AutoDesign, a framework that aligns with human design priors, where a meta-harness optimizer guides a code agent to recursively improve harness based on rollout feedback. To instantiate and evaluate this framework, we focus on the academic paper-to-poster generation task and introduce PosterBench, comprising a 100-paper Main Track spanning five disciplines and PosterBench-mini, a shared 10-paper subset for controlled evaluation. On the PosterBench Main Track, AutoDesign achieves the highest score of 78.32, surpassing the closed-source commercial system Claude Design by 7.45 points. Across seven controlled code-agent-model configurations, integrating the learned DesignHarness consistently improves performance, increasing the average PosterBench Score from 54.99 to 67.39 (+12.4%). In a fully autonomous long-horizon loop, it executes 253 tool calls and 11 editing turns within 40 minutes for under $3, reaching average conference-poster quality in human evaluation. A system-blind human study further demonstrates that AutoDesign achieves the highest human preference among evaluated systems.

AI.tldr: AutoDesign is a framework for transforming multimodal sources into structured outputs via a meta-harness optimizer that recursively improves a code agent's harness based on rollout feedback. Evaluated on academic paper-to-poster generation with PosterBench, it surpasses Claude Design by 7.45 points, boosts average scores from 54.99 to 67.39 across seven configurations, and achieves the highest human preference in blind studies.
AI.motivation: Existing model-harness systems for multimodal-to-structured-output generation are static and fail to align with human design priors or accumulate reusable experience through empirical exploration for recursive self-improvement.
AI.method: AutoDesign employs a meta-harness optimizer that guides a code agent to recursively improve its harness based on rollout feedback. A new benchmark, PosterBench (100 papers across five disciplines) and PosterBench-mini (shared 10-paper subset), is introduced for controlled evaluation.
AI.result: AutoDesign achieves 78.32 on PosterBench Main Track, surpassing Claude Design by 7.45 points. Across seven code-agent-model configurations, the learned DesignHarness increases average score from 54.99 to 67.39 (+12.4%). In autonomous mode, it completes 253 tool calls and 11 editing turns in 40 minutes for under $3. A system-blind human study confirms highest human preference.
AI.conclusion: AutoDesign demonstrates that a learnable, recursively self-improving harness system can significantly outperform static paradigms, achieving near conference-quality poster generation autonomously and cost-effectively.
